[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r12] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | People were commanded to give away surplus until alms tax was prescribed; consensus holds zakat rules specify dues on the kinds of property.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r13] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Exegetical reports describe earners keeping enough income and owners of gold and silver keeping a year's provision, then donating the remainder.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine causes enmity and hatred and obstructs reason, by which one distinguishes things and recognizes duties toward the Creator.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Gambling breeds enmity and hatred, and transfers a person's property to another without compensation.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine's benefits include pleasure and profit from trading in it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Gambling can bring a person property without toil or effort.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The sin in wine and gambling outweighs their benefits.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Both accusative and nominative are possible for al-ʿafw when mā-dhā is treated as one noun and al-ʿafw is referred back to it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | If mā is a noun and dhā a predicate meaning alladhī, al-ʿafw is nominative as the answer to what they spend.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw may be accusative as the object of yunfiqun: spend the surplus, even when mā is a noun by itself.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The clarification about wine and gambling exemplifies how God makes His signs clear.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The Prophet's address also addresses his community; singular address followed by a plural is common in Arabic and frequent in the Qur’an. | mentions 65:1
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | A plural group can be treated as a collective tribe and referred to with singular dhālika; the Qur’an likewise uses dhālika after addressing the Prophet's wives with minkunna. | mentions 33:30
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | In this world and the next may attach to you reflect, meaning reflect on the affairs of both worlds.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Alternatively, in this world and the next may attach to God clarifies the signs, meaning signs concerning both worlds are clarified so people reflect.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر | reports | Umar repeatedly prayed for clarification about wine; revelation progressed from 2:219 to the prayer restriction in 4:43 and the final prohibition in 5:90-91, after which he declared that they abstained because wine wastes wealth and reason. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the statement about sin and benefits in this verse was abrogated by the final prohibition in 5:90. | mentions 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar recounts three stages: this verse, then the ban on approaching prayer intoxicated, then the final prohibition, which the Prophet announced as making wine forbidden. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar says wine's prohibition concerned products of grapes, honey, dates, wheat, and barley, and defines wine as whatever overwhelms the intellect.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports that people drank wine after the initial verse, then left it when the prohibition in al-Ma'ida was announced; their drink was date nabidh called fadikh. | mentions 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab explains the name wine by saying its clear part rises while its dregs sink.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar defines maysir as gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid defines maysir as gambling and connects its name to the expression about staking or dividing a camel.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عبد الله بن مسعود، ابن عباس، عطاء، طاووس، سعيد بن جبير، الحسن، ابن سيرين، قتادة، مقاتل، السدي، عطاء الخراساني | reports | Abu Muhammad reports these authorities as agreeing with Mujahid that maysir means gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · النبي، أبو موسى الأشعري | reports | The Prophet says to avoid marked dice used for casting lots, since they are maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عبد الله بن مسعود، علي، ابن عمر، عائشة | reports | Ibn Masud calls dice non-Arab maysir and warns against them; Ali, Ibn Umar, and Aisha are reported similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali says chess is a form of maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab says a form of pre-Islamic maysir was selling meat for one or two sheep.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · القاسم بن محمد | reports | Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad says backgammon is maysir whenever it distracts from remembrance of God and prayer.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الأعرج | reports | Al-Araj defines maysir as casting arrows for stakes of property and fruit.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · النبي | reports | A report from the Prophet lists betting over pigeons, gambling, and throwing dice as three forms of maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says their great sin is the religious loss incurred by buying them.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains their sin as neglecting prayer and remembrance of God through wine and gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the benefits of wine are the pleasure and joy people get from drinking it.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains the benefits as the price of wine and the camel meat people obtained through gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن أبي زائدة | reports | A transmission from Mujahid through Ibn Abi Zayda differs, identifying the benefit as wine's price before prohibition.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · شبل، ابن جريج | reports | Shibl and Ibn Jurayj support the report that the benefits included what people obtained from the camel.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the verse censured wine and gambling for their greater sin without yet forbidding them; Muslims then drank wine lawfully for its benefits.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas di

[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says their sin outweighs their benefits because of the loss to religion, despite the pleasure and enjoyment people gain.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مقاتل بن حيان | reports | Muqatil contrasts the greater sin after prohibition with the benefits they had before prohibition.

[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس، عبد الله بن عمر، مجاهد، عطاء، الحسن، عكرمة، محمد بن كعب، قتادة، القاسم، سالم، سعيد بن جبير، عطاء الخراساني، الربيع بن أنس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains al-afw as what remains after providing for one's family; many listed authorities are reported similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · طاوس عن مجاهد | reports | A report through Mujahid from Tawus defines al-afw as the easy or readily available portion of everything.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | Al-Rabi explains al-afw as the good portion of one's wealth, its best and finest part.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد عن قيس المكي | reports | A report through Qays al-Makki says Mujahid defined al-afw as the obligatory charity.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says al-afw is surplus wealth and that this instruction came before charity was prescribed.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي، عطاء الخراساني، أبو محمد | reports | Al-Suddi interprets al-afw as surplus wealth and says the command was abrogated by zakat; Ata al-Khurasani is reported similarly.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan takes the instruction to mean: spend the surplus.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The reflection invited here concerns both worldly life and the Hereafter.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | Al-Ḥaramayn and Abū ʿAmr read kabīr, while the Kufans read kathīr; kabīr is preferable, matching ṣaghīr/kabīr and the established pair kabāʾir/ṣaghāʾir. | mentions 4:2
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | The Ḥaramayn and Kufans read al-ʿafw accusative, while Abū ʿAmr, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read nominative; both are grammatical, but the verse’s interpretation favors accusative.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | If dhā means “that which,” nominative is preferred but accusative is allowed; if mādhā is one word, accusative is preferred but nominative is allowed. Both occur in the question ماذا تعلمت أنحوا أم شعرا.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains al-ʿafw as the surplus.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The reading with bāʾ, kabīr, is supported by the next phrase's akbar rather than akthar.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The reading with thāʾ, kathīr, suits the counted items of consumed wine and gambling; a verse elsewhere uses akthar for degree or amount. | mentions 6:59
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | With rafʿ, mā and dhā are separate: dhā is relative, and al-ʿafw is the predicate answering what they should spend.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | With naṣb, mādhā is one interrogative word and al-ʿafw is the object of yanfiqūn.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Mā and dhā combine because both are general and ambiguous, covering rational and non-rational things; man is restricted to rational beings, so man and dhā do not combine.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr with thāʾ; the rest read kabīr with bāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سعيد عن قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the verse condemned wine without prohibiting it while it was lawful; the prayer and later al-Māʾida verses then prohibited every amount. | mentions 4:43
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أهل النظر | reports | Some scholars infer prohibition because God forbids sin in 7:33 and this verse calls wine and gambling a great sin. | mentions 7:33
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī also reads the sin as arising in deeming wine and gambling lawful; only some qualities of otherwise ordinary things are forbidden.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa says looking at wine for sensual enjoyment is itself forbidden.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The sin refers to sinful acts committed through wine and gambling and the causes leading to them.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · بعض نقلة الآثار | reports | Transmitters report that this verse descended without prohibiting wine; reports differ on whether prohibition came here or in al-Māʾida.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p309/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī says ithm can denote appropriated property; ‘sin or offense’ distinguishes a wrong against God from a wrong against people, and the verse arose over theft. | mentions 4:112, 5:107
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p310/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Taʾaththama and taḥawwaba mean avoiding sin although their forms might suggest committing it, like tafawwaqa and tajarraʿa.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Labīd’s h-j-d forms contrast sleeping with staying awake; the Qurʾān uses tahajjud for night prayer, illustrating the specialized sense. | mentions 17:79
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | prefers | Al-Fārisī favors kabīr: great sin contrasts with small sin, matching kabāʾir and akbar; great sin is also ʿaẓīm, while kathīr would contrast with qalīl. | mentions 54:53, 53:32, 4:31, 31:13, 4:48
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The thāʾ reading is supported by the warning that wine and gambling produce enmity and obstruct remembrance and prayer. | mentions 5:91
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The Prophetic report about ten persons involved with wine being cursed supports the kathīr reading.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أنس بن مالك عن النبي | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet cursed ten people involved in wine, including buyers, sellers, producers, carriers, servers, and those who consume its price.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Even if harms arise from effects of wine and gambling, revelation assigns blame to them; gambling includes wrongful taking of wealth. | mentions 5:91, 4:29
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Since sin is balanced against benefits, kathīr naturally means many harms, like the Qurʾānic description of numerous livestock benefits. | mentions 23:21
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Wine is not linguistically identical to nabīdh; primary names are not assigned by analogy, as Abū al-Aswad’s poem calls wine its sister.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Abū ʿAmr alone reads al-ʿafw nominative; others read it accusative, also reported from Ibn ʿĀmir. A Meccan transmission from Ibn Kathīr has nominative, though Meccans now read accusative.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās defines al-ʿafw as what remains beyond the family’s needs.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عطاء وقتادة والسدي | reports | ʿAṭāʾ, Qatāda, and al-Suddī define al-ʿafw as surplus.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says it is the non-straining good surplus of one’s wealth, excluding the principal.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda defines it as affordable capacity or moderation and connects it to what is clear or available.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · غيره | reports | Another authority glosses al-ʿafw as wealth beyond one’s exertion.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Mādhā can be one compound interrogative noun; retaining the alif in ʿammā dhā tasʾalu shows mā is not word-final, unlike ʿamma and fīma. | mentions 78:1, 79:43
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Alternatively, dhā can mean ‘that which’; a cited poem uses mādhā in that sense.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In the poet’s question about the women, mādhā functions like mā alone; parsing dhā as a relative pronoun is unnatural.
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Wine and gambling are described as matters of conjecture and deception.
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · طاوس وسالم | reports | On 36:55, they remarked that knowing whom the people of Paradise were distracted from would have changed how they enjoyed their occupation. | mentions 36:55
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Some people become transformed by the Divine Presence without realizing it.

[THALABI:v2p141/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The source describes staged prohibition: an earlier Meccan verse mentioned intoxicating drink from dates and grapes, when Muslims still drank lawfully; 2:219 then identified the greater sin. | mentions 1

[THALABI:v2p141/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said God was moving toward prohibiting wine; some abandoned it, while others continued for its benefits and tried to avoid its harms.

[THALABI:v2p143/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The morning after Hamza's drunken attack, he apologized; the Prophet said he had asked God, who had forgiven him.
[THALABI:v2p143/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · سعد بن أبي وقاص | reports | Atban's feast included wine and drunken boasting; Saʿd recited a poem insulting the Ansar, and an Ansari wounded him with a camel jawbone.
[THALABI:v2p143/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | After Saʿd complained, Umar prayed for a clear ruling; final prohibition came in al-Maida days after the Trench, and Umar declared they had stopped. | mentions 5:90
[THALABI:v2p143/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس | reports | Anas says wine was cherished but, at its prohibition, people poured it into streets or broke and washed vessels; after rain Medina's alleys smelled of wine. | mentions 5:90
[THALABI:v2p143/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان الثوري وأبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف وأكثر أهل الرأي | reports | This legal school narrowly defines khamr as naturally fermented grape or date juice, without fire; other drinks are not khamr by name.

[THALABI:v2p144/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Ibn Sirin reports Umar told an official to cook the drink until two-thirds evaporated, leaving one share for people and removing the devil's two shares.

[THALABI:v2p144/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عبد الرحمن السدي | rejects | Al-Suddi calls that hadith munkar: Abu al-Ahwas erred, Samak's companions did not rely on him, and Samak was weak and accepted prompting.
[THALABI:v2p144/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · أحمد | rejects | Ahmad says Abu al-Ahwas erred; Sharik differs in chain and wording, reporting that the Prophet prohibited several vessel types.
[THALABI:v2p144/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · قرصافة عن عائشة | reports | They also invoke a report attributed to Aisha through Qursafa that permits drinking if one does not become intoxicated.
[THALABI:v2p144/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports a story that Noah and Satan disputed ownership of the grapevine and settled that Noah would have one-third and Satan two-thirds.
[THALABI:v2p144/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib identifies the drink Umar permitted as one cooked until two-thirds evaporated and one-third remained.
[THALABI:v2p144/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · موسى الأموي | reports | Musa al-Umawi is reported to have drunk tala after two-thirds evaporated and one-third remained.
[THALABI:v2p144/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says tala cooked down to one-third is unobjectionable; al-Miswar agrees.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p155/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Readers pronounce al-ʿafw accusative or nominative; with mā-dhā as one interrogative, it is object and the answer is accusative.

item.text: The early notes cluster around the scope of *khamr* and *maysir*, the timing of prohibition, the harms and benefits, and the meaning and grammar of *al-ʿafw*. I’m also keeping the distinct reports and reading arguments separate.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the verse censured wine but did not prohibit it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيس بن سعد | reports | Qays b. Saʿd interprets “the surplus” to be the obligatory alms tax.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور العلماء | reports | Most scholars interpret the spending requested here as voluntary expenditure.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | Some say the command to spend the surplus was abrogated by the later zakat obligation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · آخرون | reports | Others hold the verse remains in force and establishes a claim on wealth beyond zakat.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p294/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is what one can give without exhausting oneself or one’s assets: spend what remains after needs, without making oneself dependent; the term derives from abundance.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The question about what God sent down is cited as a parallel for reading ذا as a relative pronoun. | mentions 16:24
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A further derivation connects maysir to ease, since people joined to make sharing the camel easier, though they did so by gambling.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw means increase or surplus, as in the description of a people increasing in number.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Sībawayh allows ذا to mean الذي only in this construction; the Kufans permit it elsewhere and cite poetry and Moses' question, but Tabrisi rejects their evidence because the quoted phrases may be circumstantial expressions.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | rejects | The Kufan evidence from Moses' question does not establish a relative-clause use, since بيمينك may be a circumstantial phrase. | mentions 20:17
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Khamr derives from covering: foliage, a head covering, a concealing crowd, something mixed into a disease, and covering a vessel all illustrate the root.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · كثير | reports | The poet Kathīr uses مخامر for an affliction that mingles or remains mixed in, illustrating the root sense of khamr.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A small palm-fiber prayer mat is called khumra because it covers the face from the ground during prostration.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj recounts that Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī realized an intoxicant sold under another name was wine's sibling; he cited a poem saying both were nursed by the same mother.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Maysir is gambling, named from yusr because the winner's share becomes due; the gambler is called yāsir because lots determine what is owed.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another derivation links maysir to division: whatever is divided is yassartahu; yāsir and maysir can also name the camel being divided.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw can denote excess; the cited description of sheep as fat-rich supports the sense of surplus.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وقتادة والحسن | reports | Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masʿud, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Hasan say maysir means all gambling; Imami reports count children’s nut games as gambling too.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Kabir here means a great and abundant burden of sin.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Wine’s benefits were its sale proceeds and the pleasure, exhilaration, and strength people thought drinking brought.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Gambling’s benefit was winning another person’s money without labor or hardship, with the winner able to support the poor.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Their sin outweighs their worldly benefit because it incurs God’s displeasure in the afterlife, leaving only a small, impermanent gain.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan infers prohibition because harm exceeds benefit and because the verse calls it sin, which another verse forbids; its description as a major sin independently supports prohibition. | mentions 7:33

I, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw can also mean what is left or relinquished; the Prophet’s waived horse alms illustrate property one can dispense with. | mentions 2:178
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The governing word for “in this world and the hereafter” is يبين; it may instead depend on تتفكرون.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · جماعة من الصحابة | reports | A group of Companions asked the Prophet about wine and gambling because they destroy reason and strip away wealth; this verse was revealed in response.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The apparent sense in Imami reports, also adopted by al-Shafiʿi, is any intoxicating drink that covers the mind; even a little is forbidden if much intoxicates.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#3/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa restricts khamr to grape juice once it ferments and becomes strong.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Wine is called ithm in Arabic, as the cited poem shows; the verse’s description of it as a great sin also supports prohibition.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو جعفر الباقر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir says al-ʿafw is what remains after a year’s provisions; he says the zakat verse abrogated this, as al-Suddi also held.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A fourth, unattributed interpretation takes al-ʿafw to mean the finest and best property.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The demonstrative’s kāf is singular because the address is to the Prophet, while including the community.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another construal makes the address “thus, people of this group.”
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The signs are proofs concerning spending, wine, and gambling.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another explanation takes the signs to mean all the rulings of Islam.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Here “this world and the hereafter” means their affairs.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r17] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Pondering worldly and afterlife affairs shows that this life is trial, hardship, and passing, while the afterlife is recompense and permanence, prompting renunciation of one and desire for the other.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r18] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Alternatively, “in this world and the hereafter” attaches to “He makes clear”: God explains signs in those matters so people ponder, showing He intends reflection whether or not they actually reflect.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Calling the sin great is itself evidence of prohibition, since a major sin is prohibited without disagreement.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak reads the comparison across time: after prohibition, their sin is greater than their benefit before prohibition.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr says both refer to the pre-prohibition period: the sin caused by them exceeds their benefit.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says this verse does not establish prohibition; al-Maʾida 5:90 does. | mentions 5:90
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The question means, “What thing should they spend?”
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · عمرو بن الجموح | reports | ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh asked what should be spent in jihad; another report says the question concerned charity.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس وقتادة | reports | Ibn Abbas and Qatada interpret al-ʿafw as what remains beyond family needs and sufficiency.
[TABRISI:2:219-220#4/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن وعطاء | reports | Al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ take al-ʿafw as the moderate amount, avoiding extravagance and stinginess; this is also transmitted from Abu Abd Allah.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The Kufans count two verses across 2:219–220 and treat تتفكرون as a verse ending; the other regional count has one verse and does not count that word as a verse ending.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The single-expression analysis is illustrated by the idiom عما ذا تسأل and a poem asking ماذا بال نسوتكم, meaning ما بال نسوتكم.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | For nominative العفو, ذا means الذي, so the question means what is it that they spend; العفو answers as the predicate of an omitted subject.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · أهل الكوفة غير عاصم | reports | Kufan readers other than ʿĀṣim read إثم كثير with thāʾ, while the other readers use bāʾ and read إثم كبير.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr alone reads العفو in the nominative; the other readers use the accusative.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī supports كبير because كبير contrasts with صغير, while كبير denotes a grave sin; Qur'anic examples use صغير and كبير and call grave sins كبائر. The comparison أكبر also supports كبير rather than كثير.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The كبير reading is supported by Qur'anic wording about every small and great matter being recorded and by references to major sins. | mentions 54:53, 4:31, 42:37
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The كثير reading is supported by the following verse's account of Satan causing enmity and obstructing prayer and remembrance through wine and gambling, and a report that the Prophet cursed ten involved with wine.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The argument for كثير cites the Qur'anic description of Satan's effects through wine and gambling. | mentions 5:91
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic report curses ten wine-related parties: buyer and recipient, presser and commissioner, server and requester, carrier and recipient, and the consumer of its price.
[TABRISI:2:219-220/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | For accusative العفو, ما ذا is one interrogative expression and ماذا ينفقون functions like ما ينفقون, asking what they spend; the answer is accusative.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p154/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | Āyāt can mean commands and prohibitions that God makes clear.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p436/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | ʿAfw can mean pardon, as in God’s forgiving a servant.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p436/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | ʿAfw can mean disappearance of a trace, as when dust covers and hides a dwelling’s remains.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p436/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · ابن فارس | reports | Ibn Fāris says ʿafw is lawful, good wealth; ʿafāt are petitioners, and ʿafw of wealth is what remains beyond expenses.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p436/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | ʿAfw can mean the surplus wealth available after one’s needs. | mentions 7:199
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | One occasion report says ʿUmar asked God to give a decisive clarification about wine, after which this verse was revealed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الأنصار وعمر ومعاذ | reports | Another occasion report says a group of Anṣār, including ʿUmar and Muʿādh, asked the Prophet for a ruling because wine removes reason and takes away wealth; this verse was revealed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · محمد بن القاسم | reports | Three etymologies are reported: wine is called khamr because it mixes with the intellect, covers it, or veils it.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says khamr is what covers the intellect; khimār can mean a crowd in which one is hidden, and a woman’s head covering is named for covering.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says the named wine is the agreed-upon kind, and by analogy every drink that acts like it shares its prohibition.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Scholars agree all gambling is forbidden; the verse names maysir as an example, though strictly maysir applies to gambling over camels.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وقتادة | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Hasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and others define maysir as gambling.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba derives the word from yāsara, drawing lots with arrows; the person who draws is called yāsir, yāsirūn, yusr, or aysār.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p239#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | In winter hardship, wealthy men slaughtered a camel and divided it into shares by drawing arrows; winners gave shares to the needy, the benefit named in the verse, and people praised participation and condemned refusal.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Most reciters read kabīr with bāʾ; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr with thāʾ.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · سعيد بن جبير، الضحاك، مقاتل | reports | One reading compares post-prohibition sin with pre-prohibition benefit.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن جبير | reports | Another reading compares sin and benefit before prohibition: the sins arising from their causes already outweighed their benefits.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن جبير | reports | Ibn Jubayr says wine had been permitted under the verse about drink made from date palms and grapes. | mentions 16:67
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another account says wine was permitted by the earlier divine law and Muslims remained under that rule until prohibition.

14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي عن أشياخه، سعيد بن جبير، مجاهد، قتادة، مقاتل | reports | One position says the verse censures wine without prohibiting it, so this verse was abrogated.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · جماعة من العلماء | reports | Another position finds a prohibition here because sin is forbidden by 7:33; al-Zajjāj transmits this view and Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā prefers it. | mentions 7:33
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r16] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · بعض أهل المعاني | reports | They argue that the first clause balances sin with benefit, but saying sin is greater makes sin dominant and its benefit negligible by comparison, so the prohibitive side prevails.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | One account says wine's sin is that drinking it diminishes one's religion.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي عن أشياخه | reports | Another account says drinkers become intoxicated and harm people.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Wine's sin includes enmity, hatred, and covering the faculty of reason that enables discrimination.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Gambling distracts from remembering God and prayer and causes enmity.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي عن أشياخه | reports | Another view is that gambling invites injustice and withholding what is due.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The different harms mentioned for wine and gambling may all be intended together.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Wine benefits people through profit from its sale and bodily enjoyment.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p240/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Gambling's benefit is that a person can acquire money without effort.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Gambling follows the same disagreement as wine; if this verse prohibits wine, it prohibits gambling too, while on the disapproval reading al-Māʾida explicitly prohibits gambling. | mentions 5:90
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عطية عن ابن عباس | reports | Another interpretation is whatever amount people willingly give, whether little or much.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن، عطاء، سعيد بن جبير | reports | A third interpretation is a moderate amount between extravagance and stinginess.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid interprets al-ʿafw as the obligatory charity.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · طائفة من المفسرين | reports | A fifth interpretation is property whose amount is not apparent, drawing on the phrase for a trace that has vanished.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي عن أشياخه | reports | Al-Suddī's authorities say the spending command was abrogated by the zakat obligation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Others deny abrogation; the author distinguishes the rulings by the interpretation: a required surplus or pre-zakat charity was abrogated, while zakat itself or recommended charity remains operative.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the person who asked what to spend as ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Here spending means charitable giving and a donation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Abū ʿAmr reads al-ʿafw in the nominative; the other reciters read it in the accusative.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو علي | reports | The accusative treats mādhā as accusative and al-ʿafw as its answer, as in answering “What did you spend?” with “a dirham.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | The nominative treats dhā as a relative pronoun rather than treating mādhā as one word; the answer then supplies what God sent down.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-ʿafw can mean abundance or surplus; its root usage includes something that has grown, and it can mean what comes without effort.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Al-ʿafw means what is readily available, obtained easily without coercion or hardship.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p242/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مقسم عن ابن عباس | reports | One interpretation is what remains after a person and their dependents have what they need.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p243/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Although the address is plural, al-Zajjāj says the collective means a group or community, as if addressed as a tribe.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p243/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Alternatively, the k-prefix may address the Prophet, whose address includes his community.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p243/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī says “thus” points back to the explanation of spending: in the same way, God makes the signs clear.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p243/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Alternatively, “thus” need not point back to the preceding material and simply means “in this way.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p243/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Reflecting on this world and the next lets people recognize their difference and act for the one that lasts.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p31/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi distinguishes four answer forms: replies introduced by qul, by fa-qul, questions with no stated answer, and answers without either formula; he illustrates them with the cited questions. | mentions 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1, 18:83, 10:53, 4:176, 2:186, 7:187, 20:105
[RAZI-FULL:v22p31/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The explicit command qul functions as a seal confirming Muhammad's prophethood and honoring him as God's addressee for delivering revelation. | mentions 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1, 18:83, 10:53, 4:176
[RAZI-FULL:v6p35#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi defines wine broadly: every intoxicating drink is khamr.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p35#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa defines khamr narrowly as strong grape juice that has thrown up foam.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك وجمهور أصحابه | holds | For animals and meat of the same species, Mālik and most companions classify the exchange as muzābana, uncertainty, and gambling: meat yield is unknown and meat cannot be exchanged unequally.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | holds | Mālik treats all edible quadrupeds, including camels, cattle, sheep, and game, as one genus, barring exchange of any for meat from that genus.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | holds | Mālik treats all birds as one genus and all fish as one; one report from him singles out locusts as their own category.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Mālik transmits from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, that the Prophet forbade selling an animal for meat.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | reports | Abū ʿUmar knows no established connected chain for the prohibition; its best chain is Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib's mursal report as Mālik gives it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | holds | Although al-Shāfiʿī generally rejects mursal reports, he examined Saʿīd's and found most sound; he applies the prohibition generally across animal and meat kinds and will not qualify the text by analogy without a specific report or consensus.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | holds | For al-Shāfiʿī, animal includes all creatures living on land or in water regardless of species, just as food names every edible or drinkable thing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Wine's sin includes quarrels, abuse, indecent and false speech, loss of reason needed to know duties to God, missed prayers, and distraction from God's remembrance.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عثمان | reports | Al-Nasāʾī transmits from ʿUthmān the warning that wine is the mother of evils, illustrated by a devout man lured by a woman who offers sex, wine, or killing a boy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي والليث بن سعد | holds | Al-Shāfiʿī, his companions, and al-Layth ibn Saʿd prohibit exchanging meat for a live animal in all cases, whether species match or differ, relying on the hadith's general wording.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | A report from Ibn ʿAbbās recounts that Abū Bakr refused a man's request to exchange a share from a ten-part camel for a sheep.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | holds | Al-Shāfiʿī says he knows no Companion who disagreed with Abū Bakr's refusal of the exchange.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | reports | Abū ʿUmar notes a report from Ibn ʿAbbās permitting sale of a sheep for meat, but judges it weak.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | ʿAbd al-Razzāq transmits through al-Thawrī and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib disliked selling a live animal for a slaughtered one; Sufyān says his group sees no problem.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سفيان | holds | Sufyān's own position is that exchanging a live animal for slaughtered meat is unobjectionable.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المزني | holds | Al-Muzanī says analogy permits animal for meat if the hadith is not sound, but if sound, analogy falls and the report must be followed.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#4/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | prefers | Abū ʿUmar acknowledges the Kūfans' many analogical arguments for permissibility, but says sound transmitted evidence overrides analogy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عثمان | reports | In the continuation of ʿUthmān's report, the man chooses wine, drinks until he commits adultery and kills the boy, showing how wine leads to grave acts.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · راو غير مسمى | reports | A report says al-Aʿshā was persuaded on his way to Medina to return because he would not give up wine; he planned to drink for a year first, then fell from his camel and died before reaching home.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · راو غير مسمى | reports | The account says Qays ibn ʿĀṣim gave up wine after drunkenly groping his daughter, abusing his parents, speaking at the moon, and giving wealth to a wine seller.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيس بن عاصم | reports | The poem first attributed to Qays condemns wine for ruining the intelligent, disgracing drinkers, and bringing great harm; it vows never to drink or pay for it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | reports | Abū ʿUmar cites Ibn al-Aʿrābī from al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī, who attributes those verses instead to Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Abū Miḥjan famously wished to be buried by a vine; ʿUmar repeatedly flogged him for drinking and exiled him, later ordering Saʿd to detain him, but released him from chains after his courage at al-Qādisiyya.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو محجن الثقفي | reports | After ʿUmar released him, Abū Miḥjan vowed never to drink again and kept the vow; another version says he drank when the penalty purified him but stopped once he was disgraced.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#5/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الهيثم بن عدي | reports | Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī says an informant saw Abū Miḥjan's grave in Azerbaijan or near Jurjān, with three fruiting vines growing over it and an inscription naming him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Drunkards become a joke to sensible people and may play with or wipe themselves with urine and feces; one prayed to be among the repentant and pure while wiping his face, and another thanked a dog licking him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Four arrows had no shares: al-maṣdar, al-muḍaʿʿaf, al-munīḥ, and al-safīḥ; another account lists three blanks, adding al-waghd, to prevent the drawer favoring anyone.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The drawer, also called the distributor or striker, drew from the covered arrow container while a watcher stood behind to prevent favoritism.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Gambling breeds enmity and hatred because it consumes another person's wealth wrongfully.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | The soundest account of wine's worldly benefit is trade profit: merchants brought it cheaply from Syria and sold it at high prices in the Hijaz, where buyers did not bargain.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Other claimed benefits were aiding digestion and strength, sexual vigor, generosity, courage, clearer complexion, and pleasure.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · حسان بن ثابت | reports | Ḥassān ibn Thābit's poem depicts drinking as making the drinkers kings and lions who do not flinch from battle.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شاعر غير مسمى | reports | An anonymous poem says the drinker imagines himself lord of the Khawarnaq and Sadīr palaces, but sober owns only a small sheep and camel.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Maysir offered a share without work: the group bought a camel, winners received meat without paying, while the final loser paid the full price and got no meat.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another view says gambling helped the poor because winners did not eat their shares but distributed the camel's meat to people in need.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#6/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The lottery used eleven arrows; seven marked arrows had graded shares: al-fidh, al-tawʾam, al-raqīb, al-ḥalis, al-nafis or al-nafiz, al-misbal, and al-muʿallā. Al-Aṣmaʿī says their shares totaled twenty-eight portions.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · متمم بن نويرة | reports | Mutammim ibn Nuwayra's verse calls a person who refuses to sponsor the winter camel slaughter a baram, a disfavored miser.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · لبيد | reports | Labīd says that when his people gamble they do not produce shameful scandals recounted at summer gatherings; nevertheless maysir remains wrongful consumption of wealth.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | God says the sin is greater and more harmful in the afterlife than the worldly benefits; the great sin is reckoned after prohibition, while the benefits were before it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr with thāʾ; the plural fits plural benefits, and the cited hadith listing ten cursed categories connected with wine supports abundant sins.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The hadith says the Prophet cursed wine and ten connected parties: its seller, buyer, a

item.text: The middle sources add legal disagreements about other intoxicants, cooked drinks, gambling games, and the amount of charity, along with several conflicting details of the camel lottery. I’m preserving those details within the relevant questions.

gent buyer, presser, commissioner, pourer, drinker, carrier, person it is carried for, and consumer of its price.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · باقي القراء وجمهور الناس | reports | The other reciters and most people read kabīr with bāʾ because drinking and gambling are major sins and the comparative akbar supports this reading.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جمهور القراء | reports | All reciters reject akthar with thāʾ in the comparison, except Ibn Masʿūd's codex, which has kathīr and akthar with thāʾ in both places.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r16] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم من أهل النظر | reports | Some legal theorists infer that 2:219 prohibits wine because it says wine contains sin, and 7:33 declares sin forbidden. | mentions 7:33
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عطية | rejects | Ibn ʿAṭiyya corrects al-Aṣmaʿī: the camel was divided into ten portions before the draw, not twenty-eight according to the arrow shares.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | After the camel was split into ten parts, each winner took the number of portions his arrow entitled him to and gave them to the poor.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabbāba can mean the quiver-like container holding the gambling arrows; sometimes the collection of arrows itself was called rabbāba. Abū Dhuʾayb compares a donkey and she-asses to a rabbāba and its drawer.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabbāba also means pledge or covenant, as an anonymous poet uses it for a bond entrusted to someone.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Sometimes people gambled for themselves, so the person whose arrow did not win paid the camel's entire price; the practice fed poor people of the clan, as al-Aʿshā's verse says.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā praises those who feed guests in winter and put food at the disposal of the gambler; another poem says loaned arrows return with food for the needy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | In the anonymous poem, al-munīḥ is a loaned arrow, smoothed by use and often winning; this is the praised loaned arrow, distinct from the blank arrow al-munīḥ.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#7/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأخطل | reports | Al-Akhṭal's verse calls the blank al-munīḥ a kar; lexicographers define it as an arrow with no fixed share unless its owner gives it something.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عطية | rejects | Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects that inference: the sin within wine is forbidden, not wine itself as the argument would require. | mentions 7:33
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | Some say the verse prohibits wine by calling it sin, and others equate wine with sin using a poet's line; al-Qurṭubī rejects both because it says wine contains sin, not that wine itself is sin. | mentions 7:33
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says this verse censures wine but its prohibition is established by another verse in Sūrat al-Māʾida; most exegetes hold this view.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمرو | reports | Most reciters read al-ʿafw in the accusative; Abū ʿAmr alone reads nominative, reports differ about Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq also read nominative.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النحاس وغيره | reports | Al-Naḥḥās and others prefer nominative if dhā means that which, and accusative if mādhā is one interrogative word; either form is acceptable, though the verse is interpreted accusatively.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Grammarians consider both case endings sound in ماذا تعلمت أنحوا أم شعرا, while the verse is interpreted with the accusative: spend the surplus.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#8/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The earlier question asks whom to spend on and is answered accordingly; this question asks how much to spend, concerning ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, who had asked about the amount. | mentions 2:215
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | After 2:215 was revealed, ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ asked how much to spend, and the answer about al-ʿafw addressed that amount. | mentions 2:215
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Others say the verse remains in force and wealth carries an additional due beyond zakat; al-Qurṭubī says the apparent evidence favors the abrogated view.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المفضل بن سلمة | reports | Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salama says God's clarification of the signs here concerns spending.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | One explanation says keep enough wealth for worldly livelihood and spend the rest for the next life; another takes the syntax as inverted and urges reflection on the world's passing nature and the afterlife's permanence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw means what is easy and readily available, what is surplus without hardship; spend what remains after needs without harming yourself and becoming dependent.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A poet's line uses al-ʿafw for leniency or what is readily given, supporting this sense of the word.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن وقتادة وعطاء والسدي والقرظي محمد بن كعب وابن أبي ليلى | prefers | Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Ibn Abī Laylā, and others say to give the surplus after dependents' needs; Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same explanation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid defines the giving as charity from a position of financial sufficiency, supported by the Prophet's saying that the best charity is what one gives when solvent.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet is quoted in two formulations: the best charity is given from financial sufficiency.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيس بن سعد | reports | Qays ibn Saʿd identifies the commanded spending as obligatory zakat, whereas the majority say it is voluntary spending.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جمهور العلماء | reports | The majority of scholars say this command concerns voluntary expenditure rather than obligatory zakat.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219#9/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī says the command was abrogated by obligatory zakat: a wealthy person kept a year's provision and gave the rest, while a worker kept one day's needs and gave the rest.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The questioners about wine and gambling are believers, as Qurtubi noted earlier.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qurtubi extends the prohibition to all gambling by consensus, since maysir originally concerned wagering on camels; by the same analogy, other intoxicants take wine’s ruling.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جمهور الأمة | reports | The majority hold that any drink whose large quantity intoxicates is forbidden in both small and large quantities, and that the prescribed penalty applies.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة والثوري وابن أبي ليلى وابن شبرمة وفقهاء الكوفة | rejects | These Kufan jurists allow small amounts of non-grape drinks that intoxicate in large amounts and deny the penalty absent deliberate intoxication; Qurtubi calls this weak and rejects it by reason and transmitted evidence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · بعض المفسرين | reports | Some exegetes say God bestowed every honor and good on this community and prescribed laws gradually rather than all at once; wine prohibition likewise came in stages.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qurtubi says this verse was the first revelation on wine; the later stages are detailed in the following segment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Khamr is named from khamara, “to cover”: it veils the intellect, just as a woman’s veil covers and anything covering something is said to khammar it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشاعر | reports | The unnamed poet’s phrase khamr al-tariq refers to a hollow or depression that conceals a wolf or other creature.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · العجاج | reports | Al-Ajjaj’s phrase al-khamr describes someone who does not move concealed, illustrating the sense of hiding.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The expression ghimār or khimār of people can mean a hidden place or a place within the crowd.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | A second etymology connects khamr with being left to mature, as dough ferments or an opinion is left to become clear.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | A third etymology derives the name from mixing with the intellect, from mukhāmarah, “mixing.”
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qurtubi says the three explanations converge: wine matures, mixes with the intellect, then covers it; concealment is the root sense.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:219/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Wine is grape juice that ferments or is cooked; any other substance that intoxicates the intellect has the same legal status.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r10] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Their sin consists in leading people to neglect what is commanded and commit what is forbidden.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r11] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr, “much,” with thāʾ instead of kabīr, “great.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r12] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Benefits include earning money, excitement, pleasure, and companionship; wine may embolden the coward, enhance manliness, and strengthen the constitution.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r13] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The harms arising from wine and gambling outweigh their expected benefits.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r16] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · عمرو بن الجموح | reports | Amr ibn al-Jamuh is said to have asked first about what to spend and whom to give it to, then about how to spend.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r17] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is the opposite of exertion: spend what is readily available without exhausting yourself.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Wine is categorically forbidden, as are all intoxicants according to most scholars.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa permits drinking fermented raisin or date infusion if boiled until two-thirds evaporates, provided the drinker does not become intoxicated.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Maysir is a verbal noun like mawʿid; gambling is so called because it takes another’s wealth easily or strips away prosperity.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:219/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The question is about engaging in wine and gambling, as shown by the answer’s reference to what is in both.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The author recounts the stages: the first Meccan verse (16:67) allowed intoxicants; after Umar and others asked about wine’s harm, this verse followed. Some drank and others abstained. | mentions 16:67
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The ruling includes all forms of gambling, such as backgammon and chess.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The question concerns the consequences of participating in drinking and gambling, as shown by the answer about sin and benefits.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their sin includes quarrels, insults, obscene speech, and falsehood.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · حمزة وعلي | reports | Hamza and ʿAli read كثير, meaning many, in place of كبير.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r14] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Wine benefits include trade and drinking pleasure; gambling may benefit the poor or bring easy money.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r15] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their sin outweighs their benefit because drinkers and gamblers commit sins in many ways.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r16] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is surplus beyond need; early Muslims had to donate surplus after retaining a year’s provisions as farmers or a day’s as artisans, until the zakat verse abrogated the rule. | mentions 9:103
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r17] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu ʿAmr reads العفو in the accusative; then ماذا is one noun as the object and the answer means they spend the surplus.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r18] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | If ما is the subject and ذا a relative pronoun with ينفقون as its clause, the answer العفو matches the question’s nominative syntax.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r19] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The kāf in كذلك modifies an omitted verbal noun in the accusative: an explanation like this explanation.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | After this verse, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf hosted drinkers; an intoxicated imam misrecited the disavowal sūra, prompting 4:43’s ban on approaching prayer while drunk. | mentions 4:43
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · عمر | reports | After ʿUtban ibn Malik’s guests became drunk, argued, and fought, Umar prayed for a clear ruling; 5:90 followed and he said they abstained. | mentions 5:90
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · علي | reports | Ali said that if wine fell into a well he would not call prayer from a minaret built there, nor graze land exposed by a dried sea where it had fallen.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Khamr is grape juice that boils, intensifies, and foams; its name means covering because it veils the mind.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Maysir is gambling, from يسر; it may be named for taking wealth easily without effort or for depriving someone of wealth.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The traditional game used ten arrows: al-fadh, taw'am, raqib, hils, nafis, musbil, and muʿalla awarded one to seven shares; manih, safih, and waghd were blanks.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | An impartial arbiter drew arrows from a bag; winners took their marked share, while blank-drawers got nothing and paid the camel’s full cost.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p104#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Winners gave shares to the poor, did not eat them, boasted of generosity, and disparaged those who declined to gamble.
[QASHANI:2:218-219/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Wine signifies caprice and love of the world; gambling signifies the soul's contrivance to secure its meager share.
[QASHANI:2:218-219/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Their sin is veiling and distance from God.
[QASHANI:2:218-219/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Their benefits are livelihood and psychic pleasure, including relief from troubling traits and worries through heedlessness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p398/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Khamr is grape juice that has boiled, strengthened, and thrown up foam; it is named from covering because it veils the intellect.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p398/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another derivation says wine is so called because it is covered and left until it ripens and strengthens.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p398/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari derives the name from wine mixing with the intellect; related verbs mean that illness mixes with something.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p398/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other derivations invoke leaving dough or an opinion until it matures or becomes clear; on these derivations خمر began as a verbal noun used as an active or passive participle.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p398/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Maysir means gambling and follows the pattern maf'il from yasara, as maw'id derives from wa'ada; yasartu al-maysir means I gambled.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The name maysir is variously derived from ease, affluence because gambling strips it away, something becoming due, or slaughtering and cutting up a camel.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Arabs played in winter hardship to provide for the poor: the players bought and slaughtered a camel, dividing it into ten shares according to Abu Amr or twenty-eight according to al-Asma'i.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The poem's use of تيسرون and يسرت supports connecting maysir with gambling.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The camel used for drawing lots was called maysir as the site of a windfall; by proximity the arrows were also called maysir.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Yusr, the participant in drawing lots, has plural aysār; anoth

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The game used ten arrows, or eleven; seven carried shares from one to seven, assigned to named arrows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The three blank arrows were al-maniḥ, al-safīḥ, and al-waghd; another count has four, adding al-masdar and al-muḍaʿʿaf.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Blank arrows increased and mixed the lots to prevent the dealer from favoring anyone; the dealer was also called the roller, drawer, or striker and was regarded as just.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The dealer knelt, covered himself with a cloth, placed the arrows in a quiver, mixed them, and drew one for each named man.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p399/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A winning arrow awarded its marked share; a blank won nothing and its holder had to cover the full cost of the camel.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | rejects | Ibn Atiyya says al-Asma'i was mistaken to divide the camel into twenty-eight portions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A winner shared his portion with the poor, ate none of it, and took pride in generosity; those who abstained were called baram and disparaged, though gamblers sometimes ate for themselves.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأعشى | reports | Al-A'sha's verse praises feeding a winter guest and providing food for the gambler, evidence of the game's association with generosity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زهير | reports | Zuhayr's verse uses baram for a man who is neither shamelessly greedy nor miserly when his companions win.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The gamblers sometimes took a portion of the meat for themselves.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p400/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Tafakkur is turning thought over a matter; fikr is the mind.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض من ألف في الناسخ والمنسوخ | reports | Some works on abrogation say most scholars regard this verse as abrogating the prior permissibility of wine, setting aside the Meccan Anʿām passage. | mentions 6:145
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن جبير | reports | Ibn Jubayr describes a staged prohibition: some abstained after this verse, while others drank for its benefits until prayer-time restriction and then the final command to avoid it. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي | reports | Makkī takes the sequence reported by Ibn Jubayr to show that this verse was abrogated by the later prohibition in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says this verse disparaged wine without yet prohibiting it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض الناس | reports | Some reject calling this abrogation of an earlier permission: wine had simply been left unaddressed, and people continued their customary practice until prohibition came.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمر ومعاذ | reports | The occasion reported is that ʿUmar and Muʿādh asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine and gambling, saying they destroy reason and strip away wealth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p402/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The question follows discussion of charitable spending and fighting because wine and gambling consume wealth that might otherwise go to charity or jihad. | mentions 2:215, 2:216
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The plural verb is used although the reported questioners were two, since Arabic can attribute one person’s act to a group.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي | reports | ʿAlī calls chess “the maysir of the non-Arabs.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القاسم | reports | Al-Qāsim says anything that distracts from remembering God and prayer counts as maysir.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl gives a four-stage sequence for wine: the palm-and-grape verse, this verse, the prayer restriction, then final prohibition; gradualism eased a people accustomed to drinking. | mentions 16:67, 4:43, 5:90
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They ask about the legal status, permissibility, and use of wine and gambling, not about what substances they are; the answer therefore addresses their ruling.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority define wine in law as anything drunk that overcomes and corrupts the intellect.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الرازي عن أبي حنيفة | reports | Al-Rāzī reports Abū Ḥanīfa’s definition of khamr as specifically what is made from grapes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · السمرقندي عن أبي حنيفة | reports | Al-Samarqandī reports Abū Ḥanīfa including grape, raisin, and date drinks, while treating corn and wheat drinks as mind-confusing foods rather than beverages.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān calls the sound report from Abū Ḥanīfa that even a drop of these drinks is khamr.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Maysir first named pre-Islamic Arab gambling; in law it covers every form of gambling, whose prohibition is agreed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي، وابن عباس، وعطاء، وابن سيرين، والحسن، وابن المسيب، وقتادة، وطاووس، ومجاهد، ومعاوية بن صالح | reports | These authorities classify every gambling game, including dice, chess, and children’s knucklebones or nuts, as maysir, except permitted horse wagers and lots for allocating rights.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p403/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك | reports | Mālik distinguishes amusement maysir, such as dice and chess, from gambling maysir, in which people wager against one another.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الربيع | reports | Al-Rabīʿ says this verse was revealed after wine had already been prohibited.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأكثرون ومجاهد | reports | Most commentators, including Mujāhid’s reported explanation, take wine’s benefit to mean profit and earnings from its trade.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأطباء | reports | Medical writers cited worldly benefits such as relief from sorrow, cheerfulness, digestion, strength, sexual vigor, generosity, complexion, and courage; they also catalogued many harms.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān’s apparent reading is prohibitive: consuming either entails grave sin, and anything sinful or containing sin is forbidden; sin outweighs benefit. | mentions 6:151
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan states the general rule that whatever contains sin is forbidden.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A cited poet calls wine “sin,” because drinking it makes the drinker lose reason; the usage reflects the sin associated with it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مخالفو التحريم | reports | Those denying that the verse prohibits argue that a forbidden thing cannot have benefits and that the Companions waited for the prayer and al-Māʾida verses before abstaining. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān answers that prohibited things may have immediate worldly benefits, and some Companions sought an unmistakable explicit command to make the prohibition unequivocal.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس والربيع | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Rabīʿ assign the sin to the period after prohibition and the benefits to the earlier period.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān prefers the apparent sense: sin and benefit are both being reported as present, and the sin is wrongdoing that brings punishment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p404/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طائفة | reports | One group identifies wine’s sins as loss of reason, verbal abuse, slander, and aggression produced by the drinker.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One stated benefit of gambling is that a winner becomes wealthy without work or exertion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبي | reports | A reading attributed to Ubayy has أقرب (“nearer”) in place of أكبر.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another claimed benefit is aid to the needy: winners of the camel-meat game distributed their share to the poor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | This verse does not address jurisprudential details such as other intoxicants, the drinker’s prescribed penalty, how flogging is done, or places to avoid striking; those belong to fiqh.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic report curses wine and the many people connected with producing, selling, transporting, serving, drinking, and profiting from it, illustrating the multiplicity of its sins.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p405/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الباقون | reports | The remaining canonical readers read كبير; Abū Ḥayyān says this is apt because drinking wine and gambling are major sins.
