[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan defines al-ʿafw as the moderate amount between extravagance and falling short.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الربيع | reports | Al-Rabīʿ glosses al-ʿafw as the good, choice, or best portion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Al-ʿafw is also explained as abundance, from the sense “they became numerous”; an anonymous poetic line is cited for this usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another lexical sense is purity or clarity: the idiom أتاك عفوا means something came to you pure and unclouded, supported by a poetic line.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the required pre-zakāt surplus was what remained above one thousand dirhams, or its equivalent in gold.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other thresholds proposed are the surplus beyond a third, or beyond a year’s agricultural subsistence, a month’s for desert folk, or a day’s for laborers; hardship led to zakāt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid identifies al-ʿafw with obligatory charity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan also defines the amount as one that does not exhaust the giver’s resources and leave him begging others.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another explanation is that sin is greater because its punishment endures while worldly benefits disappear; what lasts is greater than what passes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The spending question had already been asked; this answer now clarifies the quantity or amount to spend. | mentions 2:215
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The questioner is identified either as ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ or, more apparently, the believers collectively, as the plural verb suggests.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The spending may be for jihad or charity; most who say charity understand voluntary almsgiving.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some say the question concerns obligatory giving, specifically zakāt, whose details were later set out by the Sunna.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another view says people were required before zakāt to give earnings beyond their annual needs, and that duty was superseded by the zakāt verse.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ʿafw as what remains beyond the needs of one’s family and property.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p406/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طاووس | reports | Ṭāwūs understands al-ʿafw as an easy, modest amount that does not damage one’s wealth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report about someone offering a gold egg is followed by the warning that giving away all one’s wealth can leave one dependent; charity should come from sufficiency.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr is reported with both the accusative reading of the majority and the nominative reading of Abū ʿAmr.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān objects to Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s paraphrase “al-ʿafw is your spending,” since the question asks what is spent, not the act of spending; the mixed case combinations are permissible, not weak.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سعد | reports | Saʿd’s hadith says it is better to leave heirs wealthy than to leave them dependent on others.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī defines al-ʿafw as the opposite of exertion: spend what does not require exhausting effort or capacity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says to spend what exceeds one’s needs without depriving oneself and becoming dependent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الراغب | reports | Al-Rāghib says al-ʿafw covers both obligatory and voluntary giving and means surplus beyond comfortable means.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الماتريدي | reports | Al-Māturīdī defines al-ʿafw as the amount left over from subsistence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Most readers vocalize العفو in the accusative as the object of an omitted ينفقون; this matches ماذا as an interrogative object asking what they spend.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Alternatively, ما is a nominative interrogative subject and ذا a relative pronoun meaning “that which”; its resumptive pronoun is omitted, so the reply matches in meaning, not wording.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p407/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr reads العفو in the nominative; the preferred parsing makes it the predicate of an omitted subject and treats ما as subject with ذا relative.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The kāf in كذلك either qualifies an omitted verbal noun or, on Sībawayh’s account, functions circumstantially: God explains in a manner like that explanation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī says the demonstrative most immediately refers to the clarification of the proper amount and condition for spending.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī takes the reference to be the conclusion that giving the surplus is better than exhausting oneself in expenditure.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other possible referents include the rulings on wine and gambling, spending, fighting and the sacred month, the destination and reward of spending, or the amount to spend. | mentions 2:216, 2:217
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | It is too restrictive to make the demonstrative refer only to wine and gambling; even farther-fetched is taking it to cover every ruling mentioned earlier in the sūra.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The singular address in the demonstrative may address the Prophet, a listener, or a group; singular address to a group is Arabic usage, and لكم confirms collective address.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | لكم is governed by يبين; its lām conveys information to someone as in “I said to you,” while a causal reading is unlikely.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Here āyāt means signs and evidences; clear explanation is intended to lead people to reflect on worldly and afterlife concerns.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p408/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān prefers attaching “in this world and the next” to reflection generally, rather than limiting reflection to one particular matter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī says people should consider what concerns both abodes and choose what is best for themselves.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another explanation is that reflection concerns God’s commands and prohibitions, leading to obedience in this life and reward in the next.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المفضل بن سلمة | reports | Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salama applies reflection to spending: retain enough for worldly livelihood and give the rest for the afterlife.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس والزمخشري | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zamakhsharī explain that people should reflect on the world’s passing and the afterlife’s permanence, then work for what endures.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī also links reflection to wine’s worldly benefits and afterlife harms, and to holding back worldly means while giving for the hereafter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan attaches “in this world and the next” to God’s explaining the signs rather than to people’s reflection.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If explanation occurs only in this life, the phrase must mean signs concerning both abodes; if signs appear in both, no reinterpretation is needed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p409/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The proposed fronting-and-delaying analysis is unnecessary: لعل functions causally, so it and the locative phrase are both complements of يبين; an intervening parenthesis is another possible parsing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p410/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية ومكي | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Makkī explain that God shows believers signs in this world and the next, indicating both abodes and their standing so people will reflect.

YAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي | reports | Makkī treats الآيات as indefinite, making the two prepositional phrases descriptions of signs existing in both abodes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this a semantic paraphrase.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p410/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects saying the phrase syntactically attaches to الآيات: a noun cannot govern the prepositional phrase; it must modify the noun through an implicit participle or state.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p415/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | As wine among drinks and gambling’s food are prohibited, polytheist spouses are prohibited among those one may marry.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p417/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | As with wine and gambling, some benefit from a forbidden thing does not establish permissibility.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p431/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The believers asked the Messenger about wine and gambling as God had foretold; the answer that both involve grave sin was meant to lead them to abstain and indicates their prohibition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p431/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The sin is described as great in one reading and numerous in another; Abū Ḥayyān relates the wording to the Qurʾānic category of major sins. | mentions 4:31
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p431/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Benefits include money from trading in wine, gambling, and other gains; even prohibited things have some benefit, especially when people naturally desire them or grow accustomed to them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p431/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The sin's harm, which leads to Hell, outweighs the benefit that ends with its occasion; a rational person should avoid lasting punishment for temporary gain.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p432/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Asked what to spend, believers are told to give whatever is easy for them to part with; this reflects that religion imposes no undue hardship.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p432/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | God explains the signs as He has clarified wine, gambling, and spending, so that reflection on this world and the next may lead people to prefer the afterlife.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p434/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān praises the passage's eloquence, its joined clauses and elegant structure, and its movement from warning about disobedience at the opening to glad tidings for believers at the end.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The draw used ten lots, or eleven in one account: seven bore one through seven marked shares (الفذ، التوءم، الرقيب، الحلس، النافس، المسبل، المعلى); three blanks were المنيح، السفيح، الوغد, with an optional fourth blank called المضعف.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | They added blank lots to prevent the impartial dealer (الحرضة) from favoring anyone; he knelt, wrapped himself in a cloth, exposed his head, shook the lots in a bag, and drew one for each named person.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A marked lot won its assigned share; a blank meant the person paid toward the camel. This was done in winter scarcity, with the meat given to the poor, not eaten by participants; they took pride in it and called nonparticipants البرم.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most divided the camel into ten portions, one per lot.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī says the camel was divided by the count of marked lines, producing twenty-eight portions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls al-Aṣmaʿī's division mistaken.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author calls that correction surprising: Arabs may have divided the camel by ten lots on one occasion and by twenty-eight marked shares on another.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A noun is omitted after عن: the question concerns the ruling on wine and gambling, including permissibility or prohibition, not the substances themselves; the answer matches that understood question.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | فيهما is the fronted predicate and إثم the delayed subject. Fronting is optional because indefiniteness is also licensed by description or coordination; a noun meaning their use is omitted because sin is not inherent in the substances.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read كثير; the others read كبير. The majority form suits sin described as grave, drinking and gambling as major sins, and the seven readers' ب in وإثمهما أكبر. | mentions 4:2, 42:37
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The much-sin reading may describe the many individual sins of drinkers and gamblers, or the repeated and multiplied punishment resulting from their acts.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | It can also encompass the bad words and deeds produced by drinking, and all involved with wine from grape to consumption; the Prophet cursed wine and ten parties connected with it.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The plural benefits contrasts with singular sin, so describing the sin as many matches the collective sense. The author says each reading should be supported without weakening the other, as in the earlier ملك and مالك discussion.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the ب reading better: grave sins are called كبائر and lesser ones صغائر. He still regards the ث reading as sound, since abundance is a kind of greatness just as smallness can mean lowliness or scarcity.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Khamr properly denotes grape juice after fermentation and frothing; by metaphor it also covers any other liquid that ferments and froths.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Another derivation links maysir to yasar, slaughtering or cutting: a yāsir is the butcher who divides a camel. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the camel staked for lots was called maysir as the source of gain, then the arrows took that name by proximity.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The famous derivation connects khamr with covering: it veils the mind like a woman's veil. خامري حضاجر is an admonition to a fool to hide; the segment also cites the hadith about covering vessels and poetry using خمر الطريق for concealing vegetation.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second derivation says wine is covered until it ferments and strengthens, illustrated by the hadith about covering vessels.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī derives khamr from its mingling with the mind, as in the phrase the disease mixed with him.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A fourth derivation connects khamr with leaving something until it matures, as dough is left to rise or an opinion until its sound course becomes clear. On all four accounts it is originally a verbal noun used for an active or passive participle.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Maysir means gambling and is formed on mifʿal from yusr/yasara-yaysiru. Alqama's line uses ييسرون and another poet's uses ييسرونني as usage evidence.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The participant in drawing lots is called yusr and pluralized as أيسار; another account treats يسر as a plural of ياسر, like حرس from حارس.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One derivation takes maysir from ease, because winnings are easy to obtain; another derives it from wealth, since gambling strips a person of wealth.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:219/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مجاهد | reports | Al-Ṭabarī attributes to Mujāhid a derivation from يسر لي كذا, meaning something became due to me; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p578/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عمر | reports | In a report from ʿUmar, he repeatedly asks God for a clear ruling on wine: first this verse is revealed, then 4:43 bars approaching prayer while drunk, and finally 5:90–91 commands abstention, to which ʿUmar replies that they desist. | mentions 4:43, 5:90, 5:91
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p578/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The report is transmitted by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa’i through Israel from Abu Ishaq, and by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh through al-Thawri; Abu Zurʿa says Abu Maysara did not hear from ʿUmar, while Ibn al-Madini calls the chain sound and al-Tirmidhi authenticates it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p578/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن أبي حاتم | reports | Ibn Abi Hatim adds ʿUmar’s explanation that wine makes wealth and reason disappear.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p578/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar defines wine as anything that clouds the intellect; Ibn Kathir says the definition will be explained further in the commentary on al-Ma’ida. | mentions 5:90
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p578/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Maysir means gambling.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The word al-afw is read in both the accusative and nominative; Ibn Kathir regards both readings as sound, apt, and close in meaning.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r10] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says the best charity is given from a position of means, the upper hand is better than the lower, and one should begin with dependents.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · معاذ بن جبل وثعلبة | reports | A report reaching Yahya says Muadh and Thaʿlaba asked how much to spend given their dependents and servants, and this question occasioned the verse.

:v1p579#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains al-afw as what remains in excess of what one's household needs.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر، ومجاهد، وعطاء، وعكرمة، وسعيد بن جبير، ومحمد بن كعب، والحسن، وقتادة، والقاسم، وسالم، وعطاء الخراساني، والربيع بن أنس | reports | These early authorities also explain al-afw as the surplus, a sense Ibn Kathir says gathers the reported definitions.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · طاوس | reports | Tawus defines al-afw as a small amount of everything; Ibn Kathir includes this under the general sense of surplus.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الربيع | reports | Al-Rabiʿ also glosses al-afw as one's best and finest property; Ibn Kathir says the definitions return to the idea of surplus.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the instruction means not exhausting one's wealth and then having to ask people for help.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet tells a man to spend first on himself, then his family and child, and finally to use his judgment about any remainder.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579#2/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet's order to begin with oneself, then one's family, then relatives, and then give beyond them as one can.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Wine’s sins concern religion, while its benefits are worldly: bodily benefit, digestion, elimination, sharpening some minds, and the pleasure of intoxication; gambling winnings could also support a person or family.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · حسان بن ثابت | reports | Hassan ibn Thabit’s pre-Islamic verse depicts drinkers as becoming kings and lions undeterred by battle, illustrating wine’s intoxicating pleasure.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Other worldly gains included selling wine and spending its price, or using gambling proceeds for oneself or one’s family.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Those benefits do not outweigh the greater harm to intellect and religion; the verse prepares for wine’s categorical prohibition by implication, before 5:90–91 states it explicitly. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p579/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر، والشعبي، ومجاهد، وقتادة، والربيع بن أنس، وعبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | These authorities say this was the first verse revealed about wine; the verse in al-Nisa’ followed, then the verses in al-Ma’ida, which made wine unlawful. | mentions 4:43, 5:90, 5:91
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p580/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A prophetic saying teaches that giving away one's surplus is good, hoarding it is harmful, and a person is not blamed for retaining enough.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p580/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس، عطاء الخراساني، السدي | reports | Ibn Abbas, ʿAta al-Khurasani, and al-Suddi report the view that the command to give the surplus was abrogated by the zakat verse.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p580/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد وغيره | prefers | Mujahid and others say the command is explained by the zakat verse rather than abrogated; Ibn Kathir prefers this interpretation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p580/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | As God clarified these rulings, He clarifies the rest of His verses concerning rulings, promise, and warning so people will reflect on worldly life and the Hereafter.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p580/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir points back to the many early reports on reflection and taking lessons that he cited under the verse about signs in creation in Al Imran. | mentions 3:190
[BURHAN:v1p133/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The phrase لعلكم تتفكرون occurs twice in al-Baqara.
[BURHAN:v4p52/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The first three questions appear without conjunction because they arose at separate times; the later questions are joined with wāw because they were asked together. | mentions 2:215, 2:220, 2:222
[NASHR:v2p159/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | The joined form ماذا has six possible analyses: interrogative plus demonstrative, interrogative plus relative, compound interrogative, a single noun meaning thing, extra ما plus demonstrative, or interrogative ما plus extra ذا.
[NASHR:v2p159/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr's nominative العفو favors two words, interrogative ما and relative ذا, allowing a pause after either; other readers' accusative favors one compound word and a pause only after ذا.
[NASHR:v2p226/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Hamza and al-Kisai read إثم كثير with thāʾ; the other readers read إثم كبير with bāʾ.
[NASHR:v2p226/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr reads العفو with nominative; the other readers use accusative.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Harali calls maysir a pre-Islamic gambling institution intended to benefit the weak and to gain the spoils of victory.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Wine and gambling are paired because both undermine striving and other goods by transferring wealth without the owner's willing consent.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The author says wine and gambling are paired here as they are in the Maidah passage. | mentions 5:90
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r13] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The pronoun refers to using or consuming both wine and gambling.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r14] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The sin includes lying, abuse, loss of reason, and taking another's property; declaring the acts sinful establishes their prohibition and identifies them as major sins.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r15] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Harali notes readings with bāʾ and thāʾ, كبير and كثير, which indicate both great magnitude and large quantity of sin; either should deter a sound person.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r16] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The author frames the question and gradual explanation as an expression of divine forbearance, leaving matters beyond the subject at pure permissibility.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Wine was then allowed during the night of fasting; people commonly drank date and raisin nabīdh, which could ferment in the hot climate.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Intoxication obstructs worship, especially military striving, because a drunk person cannot contribute judgment or physical force.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Unlike food, wine was not necessary to sustain the body, so explaining its status could be deferred until more urgent matters were addressed.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The author says the intervening verses were concluded by returning to the theme of striving with which they began, before later verses on permissions. | mentions 2:218
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After discussing striving as a ground for hoping in mercy, the passage fittingly turns to what the author calls the greatest folly and sources of evils: wine and gambling.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | reports | The author says wine was among the spoils taken by Abdullah ibn Jahsh's expedition, which occasioned the preceding verses.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Harali relates khamr to covering: vegetation hides what is visible, while wine conceals the intellect and obscures the boundary between clear reason and brute animality.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p408/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Harali defines wine as anything intoxicating, whatever the drink and whether its amount is small or large.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p409/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The benefits people seek include trading in wine, enjoying its taste, winning money through gambling, aiding the poor, boasting over nonparticipants, and gaining companions and their food, drink, and gifts.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p409/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi is quoted as defining maysir as any game requiring a person to pay or receive money; chess without a wager, abusive speech, or missed prayer is not maysir.

[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r2] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · طارق بن عبد الله | reports | Tariq heard the Prophet urge charity, praise the giving hand, and tell people to begin with parents, then siblings and nearer relatives.
[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r3] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says it is sufficient sin to withhold provision from someone whose needs one controls; Abdullah ibn Amr therefore sends his steward to feed the enslaved people.
[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r4] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the signs invite reflection on this world and the next: the world's disappearance and the afterlife's enduring life.
[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r5] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says reflection on both worlds teaches the superiority of the afterlife over this world.
[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r6] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · الحسن | reports | Hasan says a thoughtful person recognizes this world as trial followed by extinction, and the afterlife as recompense followed by permanence.
[DURR-FULL:v1p610/r7] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says reflection reveals the world's trial and extinction and the afterlife's permanence and recompense, so people should set aside worldly needs for the next life.
[ITQAN:v1p79#2/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عمر | reports | Al-Tayalisi transmits Ibn Umar's account of alcohol's three-stage prohibition: first 2:219 left people free to benefit, then 4:43 prohibited drinking near prayer, and finally 5:90 prompted the Prophet to declare it forbidden. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[ITQAN:v2p305#2/r23] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | العفو means what remains in your wealth beyond what is needed.

[ITQAN:v2p421/r10] ITQAN, d. 911 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam says يقدر means “decrease” wherever it occurs in the Quran.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r11] ITQAN, d. 911 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | The same authority glosses التزكي throughout the Quran as Islam.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r12] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو مالك | reports | Abu Malik says وراء means “before” throughout the Quran, except in two verses where it means “other than.” | mentions 23:7, 4:24
[ITQAN:v2p421/r13] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو بكر بن عياش | reports | Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash distinguishes the Quranic forms كسفا: one denotes punishment and the other a piece of cloud.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r14] ITQAN, d. 911 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima distinguishes what God made from what people made using two forms of سد.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r15] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو روق | reports | Abu Rawq says every Quranic occurrence of جعل means “created.”
[ITQAN:v2p421/r16] ITQAN, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid glosses المباشرة in the Quran as sexual intercourse.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r17] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says فاسق means liar throughout the Quran, with a few exceptions.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r18] ITQAN, d. 911 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says حنيفا means Muslim and حنفاء means Muslims who are pilgrims.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r19] ITQAN, d. 911 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr gives three Quranic senses of العفو: pardoning sin, the surplus to spend here, and forbearance between people. | mentions 2:237
[ITQAN:v2p421/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says every Quranic mention of a cup means wine.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak glosses فاطر in the Quran as Creator.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr says every occurrence of إفك in the Quran means a lie.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو العالية | reports | Abu al-ʿAliya says Quranic commands to enjoin right mean Islam, while prohibitions of wrong mean worship of idols.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو العالية | reports | Abu al-ʿAliya says Quranic references to guarding sexual parts generally mean avoiding adultery.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the Quranic phrase إن الإنسان كفور refers to unbelievers.
[ITQAN:v2p421/r9] ITQAN, d. 911 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz says every mention of abiding eternally means there is no repentance.
[ITQAN:v2p516/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | For the nominative reading, al-Suyuti prefers parsing ما as interrogative and ذا as relative, yielding “what they spend is the surplus”; this matches nominal question and answer.
[ITQAN:v2p516/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | For the accusative reading, he prefers ماذا as a single interrogative form, yielding “they spend the surplus”; a verb question is answered by a verb phrase.
[ITQAN:v2p516/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | Other possible parses make ذا demonstrative, ماذا a noun meaning “something” or a relative, ما extra, or ذا extra after interrogative ما.
[ITQAN:v3p302/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · الكرماني | reports | Al-Karmani explains that four “they ask you” questions lack a conjunction because they were asked at separate times; three later questions use one because they arose together.
[SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p42/r1] SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 · author | holds | Al-Suyūṭī says the account concerning the question about wine will be given in his discussion of Surat al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90
[SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p42/r2] SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that companions ordered to spend in God's cause asked what portion of their wealth they should give; the answer was to spend the surplus.
[SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p42/r3] SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 · يحيى | reports | Yaḥyā relates that Muʿādh b. Jabal and Thaʿlaba asked what to spend from their wealth because they had dependents and families; this verse was revealed.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The cited Mathnawī couplet urges disciplining the soul away from Satan, keeping angelic company, and feeding it lawful sustenance that brings light and perfection.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Gambling could bring unearned money and meat for the poor, since winners distributed the camel's meat to people in need.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Companions were exceptionally good: they asked the Messenger only thirteen questions, all answered in the Qurʾan, and asked only about matters beneficial to them and Muslims.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The question is about the ruling on consuming wine, since permissibility, prohibition, sin, and obedience attach to accountable acts, not to objects in themselves; the ruling also covers sale and purchase.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Khamr is named from the root for covering: grape juice that boils, thickens, and foams covers the intellect and discernment, as though it were itself a veil.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Maisir is a verbal noun from yasara; it may be named for taking wealth easily without labor or for impoverishing the loser.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Maisir includes every kind of gambling, chess, and even children's games with walnuts and dice.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The phrase refers to engaging in and using wine and gambling.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds |

Their grave sin is that wine destroys reason, the pivot of religion and worldly life, and both wine and gambling ruin wealth.
[BURSEVI:v1p277#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Wine had perceived benefits including exhilaration, resale profit, strengthening the weak, aiding digestion and sex, easing grief, emboldening the fearful, loosening the miser's hand, improving complexion, and stirring speech and resolve.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Wine incites enmity and hatred and diverts from remembrance of God and prayer; it makes the sensible foolish, as illustrated by an obscene drunkard's behavior. | mentions 5:90
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Wine was prohibited in the third year after the Hijra, a few days after the Battle of the Trench.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl explains the staged ban as gentle instruction: people were accustomed to wine and benefited from it, so an immediate prohibition would have burdened them; after the final ruling, it was poured out.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar says that when the final ban came, some Companions broke their wine jars and others washed them with water and clay; rain later revealed wine's color and smell in Medina's streets for a time.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Wine had been exceptionally beloved to the Arabs, and God prohibited nothing more forcefully than it.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن أبي الدنيا | reports | Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recounts seeing a drunkard urinate into his hand, wipe his face as if performing ablution, and praise Islam and water; no grading is given.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | When a gambler loses his money without compensation, he resents the winner, becomes his enemy, and seeks to harm him.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المفسرون | reports | Commentators describe a four-stage prohibition: the first, Meccan verse mentioned wine made from dates and grapes alongside good provision, and Muslims initially drank it as lawful. | mentions 16:67
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المفسرون | reports | After ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and other Companions asked about wine because it removes reason, the verse on wine and gambling was revealed; some tried to take its benefits while avoiding its sin, while others abstained.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المفسرون | reports | At a gathering hosted by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, a drunken reciter omitted the negation in Sūrat al-Kāfirūn; the prayer-time prohibition followed. | mentions 4:43, 109:1
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المفسرون | reports | After the prayer-time restriction, some still drank outside prayer hours, expecting to sober up between the evening or dawn prayer and the next prayer. | mentions 4:43
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المفسرون | reports | At ʿItbān ibn Mālik's feast, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ recited a poem insulting the Anṣār and praising his clan; a guest struck and wounded Saʿd with a camel's jawbone, after which Saʿd complained to the Messenger.
[BURSEVI:v1p278/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · عمر | reports | After Saʿd's injury, ʿUmar prayed for a decisive clarification; the final prohibition verses were then revealed and he answered that they had desisted. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | As outward wine comes from grapes, dates, raisins, and grains, inward wine comes from heedlessness, desire, caprice, and love of the world; these intoxicate the human soul and intellect and are sinful.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reading says sins outweigh benefits because the sins affect the many while benefits belong to the elect, and the many outnumber the elect.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The charity question continues the topic of what to spend raised by the earlier verse; when 2:215 was revealed, ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ asked what he should spend, prompting the instruction al-ʿafw. | mentions 2:215
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is the opposite of effort and hardship: spend what is easy, available, and surplus to one's own needs and the needs of dependents.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The kāf is accusative as an adjective for an omitted absolute object, meaning clarification like this; singular address can target a plural audience conceived as a group.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God makes the signs concerning legal rulings clear in their import and indication, not after they were obscure or confused.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Since intoxicants are sinful, every intoxicant is forbidden, and anything whose large amount intoxicates is forbidden even in a small amount.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A different spiritual wine intoxicates hearts, spirits, and secrets: it is the drink of spiritual arrivals in cups of witnessing, poured by the cupbearer of divine attributes' self-disclosure.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | That spiritual drink quiets appetites; hearts are absorbed in ecstasies, spirits in witnessing, and secrets in the glimpse of beauty, so it is beneficial and lawful.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Some are intoxicated by the drink's existence, others by witnessing its cupbearer; a couplet contrasts their states.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | In the spiritual journey, turning away from the cups of union at the end is a greater loss than a thousand years of seeking at the beginning is a gain.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Just as a wine-drunk person is barred from prayer, one drunk with heedlessness and caprice is veiled from communion.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The inward sin of gambling is the prevalence of trickery, deception, lying, and foul speech in the way people pursue the spiritual path; it is grave to the elect and alien to the righteous.
[BURSEVI:v1p279#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The inward benefit of gambling is disregard for both worlds and effacement of worldly forms in the singularity of the Kaaba's imprint.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Thinking about both abodes means choosing what is better and easier in this life, what benefits in the next, and avoiding what harms one there.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · البغوي | reports | Al-Baghawī says to reflect on the world's passing nature and renounce it, and on the Hereafter's permanence and turn toward it.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A man offered the Prophet his only possession, a gold egg from a campaign, as charity. The Prophet first turned away, then angrily took and threw it, rebuking him for giving away all his wealth and leaving himself dependent; charity should come from surplus. No grading is given.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw also hints that a donor's gift should leave no trace in the heart, meaning it should be given freely and cheerfully; the root sense is erasure.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The elect give from wealth beyond sufficiency, while the elite of the elite practice selfless preference and give what they need, even to a wealthy recipient.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The highest form of self-preference is supported by the verse describing believers who give others priority even while themselves in need. | mentions 59:9
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar donated half his wealth to outdo Abū Bakr, but when asked what remained for his family he said half; Abū Bakr gave everything, saying Allah and His Messenger remained for them, and ʿUmar conceded he would not compete again.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A report says the Prophet described the distance between ʿUmar and Abū Bakr as like the difference between their two answers about what they left for their families; no grading is given.
[BURSEVI:v1p280/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The account shows Abū Bakr's superiority over ʿUmar in this respect, but excellence in one matter does not establish inferiority in every other matter; ranking depends on knowledge of God.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الواحدى | reports | Al-Wāḥidī says ʿUmar, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and a group of Anṣār asked the Prophet for a ruling because wine and gambling destroy reason and consume wealth; this verse was revealed.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some jurists adopt Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad’s threshold for the drinking ban as a precaution.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | In the Hanafi position and common Arabic usage, calling a drink from other substances “wine” is figurative; some people argue that the word is literal for every intoxicant.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الروايات | reports | Another account says the verse first came after the Prophet arrived in Medina; people continued drinking until ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s feast, where intoxicated ʿAlī omitted “no” while leading prayer, prompting 4:43. | mentions 4:43
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الروايات | reports | At a later feast hosted by ʿUtban, Saʿd’s boasting poem insulted the Anṣār; a man struck and wounded him, after which Saʿd appealed to the Prophet and the final prohibition was revealed days after al-Aḥzāb; ʿUmar declared they had stopped. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · علي | reports | ʿAlī says he would not pray from a minaret built over a well into which wine

 had fallen, nor let his animal graze where wine had fallen into the sea.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar says that if he dipped his finger into wine, it would not follow him, an image of complete avoidance.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام أبي حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa defines wine narrowly as grape juice that boils, ferments, and casts up foam; the term is explained as covering the mind, like a woman’s veil covers her face.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Other proposed etymologies connect wine with covering, mixing with the mind, or being left until it matures; these accounts are close in sense, and the noun may be an agent, patient, or intensive verbal noun.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمامان | reports | Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad do not require foam to appear; fermentation alone suffices because the intoxicating cause is then present.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p111#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام أبي حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa regards boiling as the beginning of fermentation and foam rising and settling as its completion; legal consequences attach to completion, as with the fixed penalty and sale prohibition.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشيخان وأبو داؤد والترمذي والنسائي | reports | Reports in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and Sunan collections state that every intoxicant is wine.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | One who denies wine’s intrinsic prohibition and says only its intoxicating effect is forbidden is an unbeliever for rejecting scripture, which calls it impurity; the cited verse is 5:90. | mentions 5:90
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A report says wine is forbidden in itself, with a version adding that its small and large amounts are alike; intoxication rules govern other drinks.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Cooking cannot erase an already established prohibition; however, a cooked drink is not subject to the fixed penalty until it intoxicates, since that penalty for a small amount applies specifically to raw wine.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Bādhq and munṣaf, grape must cooked until less than two-thirds evaporates, are forbidden if fermented and foaming; al-Alusi says their thinness, intoxication, and pleasure attract sinners, so they are banned to prevent corruption.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأوزاعي وأكثر المعتزلة | reports | Al-Awzāʿī and most Muʿtazilites permit this drink because it is pleasant and not wine; the author responds that it is intoxicating and attracts sinners, so it should be prohibited to prevent corruption.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Raw date infusion, called sakar, is forbidden; the author invokes the Companions’ consensus and the verse’s initial, pre-prohibition setting. | mentions 16:67
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · شريك | reports | Sharik argues date infusion must be permitted because the verse mentions it as a favor, which could not be forbidden; the author rejects this using consensus and the verse’s earlier setting. | mentions 16:67
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو داؤد | reports | Abū Dāwūd reports that the prohibition was revealed for wine made from five sources—grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and corn—and that wine is what clouds the mind.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو هريرة | reports | Muslim reports from Abū Hurayra that wine comes from these two trees, with the Prophet pointing to the vine and date-palm.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أنس | reports | Anas reports that grape wine was scarce when wine was prohibited and most of their wine came from unripe dates and dates.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Alusi reads these reports as teaching the legal rule that all intoxicants are forbidden, not defining Arabic vocabulary; the Prophet’s mission was guidance, while his audience already knew Arabic.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Deriving “wine” from its covering the mind does not prove that the word covers every intoxicant; “star” likewise derives from appearing but names a particular star.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | A middle position says Arabic uses “wine” literally for intoxicating grape juice and figuratively for other sources, while Islamic law made it a technical term for every intoxicant, like prayer, fasting, and alms.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The disagreement is substantial: permitting grape wine is disbelief by consensus, while permitting other intoxicants is not, since their designation as wine is disputed and their prohibition is inferential.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p112/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Grape wine itself is forbidden independently of intoxication, so all amounts, even a drop, are forbidden and its drinker is liable to the fixed penalty.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Maysir derives from taking money easily, losing wealth, dividing shares, or a stake becoming due; the gambler was called yasir because he won a share of the slaughtered camel.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wāḥidī derives maysir from something becoming due, calling the gambler the one who owes the stake.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The traditional game used ten arrows, three blank; the other seven awarded one through seven shares of a camel divided into twenty-eight parts, while a blank-draw loser paid the entire cost.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azharī gives another description of the arrow names and omits al-waghd; al-Alusi relies on the account preferred by al-Zamakhsharī and many others.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | An unnamed poet composed a mnemonic listing the ten gambling arrows and their shares, including the three blank arrows.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Maysir includes all gambling and wagering: backgammon, chess, children’s nuts and dice, risky lots outside division, and every kind of stake; Ibn Sīrīn says anything involving risk is maysir.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The question concerns engaging in wine and gambling, as the answer’s “in them” makes clear; their sin comes from leading to neglected duties and committed prohibitions.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Their benefits include pleasure, joy, digestion, improved complexion, sexual vigor, courage, generosity, and helping the weak; these benefits exist before and after prohibition, and no proof says prohibition removes them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن أبي الدنيا | reports | Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recounts a drunk man urinating into his hand and washing his face with it as if performing ablution.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One reading takes the verse about date produce as a rebuke: people make intoxicating drink from it and leave wholesome provision. | mentions 16:67
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Alusi laments that contemporary drinkers favor intoxicants other than grape wine, inventing names such as amberiyya and iksīr to imagine the new names make them lawful.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | These other drinks carry a lesser prohibition than grape wine, so permitting them is not disbelief because the ruling is ijtihād-based; declaring all permitters unbelievers would leave almost nobody.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Maysir is a verbal noun on the pattern of mawʿid or marjiʿ, used for gambling; its derivation may refer to taking wealth easily, losing wealth, dividing shares, or a stake becoming due.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأوزاعي | reports | Raw raisin infusion is forbidden once it ferments and boils, though al-Awzāʿī disputes the ruling.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبي حنيفة وأبي يوسف | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf permit lightly cooked date or raisin nabīdh, even when fermented, if the amount is thought not to intoxicate and is drunk without revelry.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · محمد والشافعي | reports | Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī forbid lightly cooked date or raisin nabīdh even in the restricted quantity described by Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام الأول والثاني | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf permit drinks made from honey, figs, grains, or grape juice cooked down by two-thirds; Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī forbid them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المتأخرون | reports | Later Hanafi jurists issued fatwas following Muḥammad’s prohibition for the other beverages; Ibn Wahbān says this ruling is also transmitted from all the imams.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Alusi’s preferred rule is that any non-grape drink is forbidden if it can intoxicate an unaccustomed drinker; a small amount is like a large one, and drinking incurs the penalty, divorce effect, and severe impurity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم | reports | In the Ṣaḥīḥayn the Prophet answers a question about honey nabīdh that every intoxicating drink is forbidden; Abū Dāwūd reports his prohibition of every intoxicant and stupefier.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p113/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم | reports | Prophetic reports say that whatever intoxicates in a large quantity is forbidden in a small quantity, and that even a palmful is forbidden if a full measure intoxicates; the author calls the r

[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · العباس بن مرداس | reports | Al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās says in the pre-Islamic period that he would not put his ignorance into his belly by drinking, nor be a leader in the morning and a fool by evening.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · معاذ بن جبل وثعلبة | reports | A report through Abān from Yaḥyā says Muʿādh and Thaʿlaba, with households and dependents, asked the Prophet how much of their wealth to spend.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This question coordinates with the earlier one as a new topic; another report links it to ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, who first asked about recipients and then about the amount to give.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The answer shows that the question asks the quality or amount of what to spend: “what” functions as a question about a description, as in asking what someone is and answering “generous.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | ʿAfw is the opposite of exertion: what remains beyond need or does not burden the giver; smooth, easy-to-tread ground is also called ʿafw.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains ʿafw as the surplus remaining after providing for dependents.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan explains ʿafw as an amount that does not strain the giver.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو هريرة | reports | The Prophet says the best charity is given from sufficiency and that one should begin with those one supports; this is reported by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasāʾī.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r17] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو هريرة | reports | Ibn Khuzayma’s version says the best charity leaves sufficiency, the upper hand is better, and one should begin with dependents; wife, slave, and child each plead for support.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r18] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جابر | reports | Jābir reports that Abū Ḥuṣayn al-Sulamī offered his only egg-sized piece of mined gold as charity; after repeatedly turning him away, the Prophet took and threw it, warning against giving everything and then begging.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Wine distracts from remembrance and prayer, commonly produces hostility and fights, deepens into addiction, and can cause illnesses and death; loss of reason and uprightness alone suffices to make it the source of vices.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said to avoid wine because it is the mother of all evils; al-Alusi adds that no prophets are reliably reported to have drunk it at any time.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Gambling takes wealth wrongfully and leads many gamblers to theft, loss of life, neglect of dependents, shameful conduct, and hidden or open enmity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some scholars infer that the verse itself prohibits wine because the greater harm outweighs its benefit; others add that “great sin” means punishment or its cause, which applies only to the forbidden.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the verse is not explicit proof of prohibition: “sin” can mean harm, and a preponderance of harm alone establishes preference, not a ban; Companions drank until the al-Māʾida prohibition. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One reading has “much sin” with thāʾ, and Ubayy reads “their sin is nearer than their benefit.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Placing sin first, describing it as great or numerous, and delaying benefits while limiting them to people signals the dominance of the harm.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p114/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن عباس | reports | Ibn Isḥāq reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that companions ordered to spend in God’s path asked how much to give; before the verse, some spent everything and then lacked food or charity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr reads “mādhā yunfiqūn” with nominative inflection, parsing the question as subject and predicate; the others read the accusative, supplying a verb with “what” as its object to match the answer.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | “Thus” may point to the explanation that surplus charity is better than exhausting one’s means because it preserves resources and benefits the afterlife; it may also encompass the whole preceding discussion.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Taking “thus” to refer only to “their sin is greater than their benefit” is remote.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The kāf is accusative as an adjective of an omitted noun, while the definite article in “the signs” is generic: God clarifies rulings by clear revelation, another verse, or the Prophet’s explanation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Although a plural form might be expected to match “for you,” the demonstrative stays singular by construing it as a collective noun with singular form, for lighter expression.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says the singular signals every recipient of the address, as in “We pardoned you after that” (2:52); al-Alusi objects that this would create multiple addressees within one uncoordinated sentence. | mentions 2:52
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p115/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Contemplating the signs means deriving rulings and understanding the interests and benefits attached to them; this makes reflection a fitting aim of their clarification.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Elmalılı says wine prohibition came in four stages: it was initially permitted, and Muslims drank while the Prophet remained silent. | mentions 16:67
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Gambling means staking money on an uncertain, risky outcome whose result is unknown, to give or receive wealth.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Pre-Islamic Arabs gambled using games learned from Arabs, Persians, and others, including backgammon and chess.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A lottery used ten named arrows to divide a slaughtered camel into twenty-eight shares, with seven arrows assigned increasing portions from one to seven.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Three arrows were blank; participants drew on one another's behalf, losers paid for the camel, and winners donated their portions to the poor.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because the lottery was treated as charity and an honorable practice despite being gambling, maysir came to denote gambling generally.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Elmalılı cites a hadith classifying children's knucklebone and walnut games as maysir.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hazret-i Ali | reports | Ali rejected a wager in which one person promised eggs to another who could eat a specified quantity, ruling that it was gambling.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | If even a lottery framed as charity is forbidden, ordinary forms of gambling are forbidden all the more.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Asking about wine and gambling together points to their customary association.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Both waste wealth and ruin people, and each commonly leads to the other; wine removes reason, enabling innumerable crimes and evils linked to gambling.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hazret-i Ömer ve Muâz ve diğer bazı ashâb-ı kirâm | reports | Umar, Muadh, and other Companions sought a ruling because wine removes reason, occasioning this verse.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Their benefits include some pleasure and enjoyment, substantial trade, courage for the fearful, strength of temperament, and windfall gains from gambling.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The gains are temporary and illusory, while losses include hangovers, disaster, ruined health, worthless profit, addiction, and individual, social, physical, and moral harm.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r22] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because preventing harm takes precedence over obtaining benefit, reason itself requires these practices to be forbidden; imagined small gains risk certain, sweeping loss.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r23] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse entails legal prohibition, but by itself does not state an unambiguous intrinsic ban; some Companions missed the legal force of its rational warning until 5:90–91 gave an explicit, absolute command. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r24] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı says the later command in 5:90–91 explicitly and absolutely forbade wine. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | This began the prohibition, but its wording still left a possibility of permissibility; some quit immediately while others continued.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hazret-i Ali | reports | Ali is reported to say he would neither pray from a minaret built over a well touched by a drop of wine nor graze animals where a wine-tainted sea had dried.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Abdullah b. Ömer | reports | Ibn Umar is reported to say he would cut off a finger that had been dipped in wine.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Maysir is a verbal noun from yusr or yasar meaning gambling,

[ELMALILI:2:219-220#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The question can ask either what causes or recipients should receive spending, or what amount or property should be spent; the first was answered earlier, the latter now.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Al-afw means spending what remains beyond one's necessary needs.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Earn wealth through lawful means, then give its surplus beyond necessities to the charitable causes already described.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Dependents include young children, a wife, needy parents, and comparable ascendants; their support counts as one's own, so charity must not leave them or oneself without necessities.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God explains legal signs and proofs so people may reflect, understand their purposes, and act on them.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı renders al-khamr as wine and al-maysir as gambling.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Grape wine and drinks made from it are intrinsically impure, and even a drop may not be consumed; impurity of other intoxicants is uncertain, so contact need not invalidate prayer.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebû Hanîfe | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa held that a small amount of non-grape intoxicant could be drunk for strength if it did not intoxicate and was not consumed to imitate immoral people or unbelievers.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | The preferred Hanafi view, shared with the other three schools, follows the hadith that whatever intoxicates in a large amount is forbidden even in a small amount.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | For the legal question of drinking, all intoxicants count as hamr in the broad sense; chemically, fermentation gives intoxicants a shared wine-like nature, reflected in the word alcohol.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Medicinal treatment follows the Qurʾanic concession for necessity, including needs treated as necessities. | mentions 2:173, 6:145, 16:115
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In the verse's translation, al-ʿafw is rendered as what does not burden or strain the giver.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and other Companions asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine because it removes the intellect; this verse was revealed.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hamr originally means covering; specifically it names fermented grape juice after its foam subsides because it covers the intellect or clouds the head.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | By extension, hamr can mean any substance that intoxicates, so all intoxicants fall under the word in its broad sense.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İbn Ömer | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that at the time the wine prohibition was revealed, hamr came from grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and millet, and meant what clouds the intellect.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Nu‘mân b. Beşir | reports | A report in Abū Dāwūd attributes to the Prophet the statement that wine is made from grapes, dates, honey, wheat, and barley.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İmam Mâlik, İmam Şâfiî and many jurists | reports | Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and many earlier and later jurists take hamr broadly as any intoxicant, making every kind Qurʾanically forbidden, including every drop and its trade. | mentions 5:90
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebû Hanîfe, his Companions and many early jurists | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and many early scholars say Qurʾanic hamr definitively means grape wine; other intoxicants are forbidden for intoxication by analogy and hadith, not by the word's certain scope.
[ELMALILI:2:219-220/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı distinguishes the definitive Qurʾanic prohibition of grape wine from the broader possible meaning: other intoxicants are prohibited through the intoxication rationale and hadith, not the wording alone.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ithm is disobedience through a corrupt act God does not approve; in legal usage it is a blameworthy act opposed to devotional obedience.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Wine's harms include excess and brawling that breed enmity, divert from God's path and prayer, impair reason, invite ridicule, and waste wealth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عمارة بن الوليد بن المغيرة المخزومي | reports | Ibn Ashur introduces Amara ibn al-Walid's poem as evidence of money spent on wine.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib suggests the derivation of ithm carries the sense of delay from good.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi defines sin as blame attached to an act, effectively the opposite of reward.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Wine and gambling cause sin through drunken excess and disputes over gambling wins and losses.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Kabir describes an immaterial sin metaphorically: it means exceptionally intense in its kind.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The figurative container preposition fi emphasizes how closely sin and benefit attach to wine and gambling, in their customary use.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling the outcome ithm signals that users incur punishment in this world and the next.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Most readers have kabir, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read kathir, using abundance figuratively for intensity of quality.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p343/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Manafiʿ may be a verbal noun whose form intensifies benefit, or a place noun denoting abundant benefit; either way it is stronger than nafʿ.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The spending question accompanied the wine-and-gambling question, so its answer is joined by waw; banning them threatened aid to the poor, making proper spending relevant.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي ﷺ | reports | A prophetic report promises reward for spending to please God, even a bite placed in one's wife's mouth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Giving from surplus does not preclude giving needed or all one's wealth if one can bear it patiently and has no dependent to support.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن أبي حاتم | reports | Ibn Abi Hatim reports that Muadh ibn Jabal and Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanima asked what should be spent.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Another view identifies Amr ibn al-Jamuh as questioner, answered in 2:215 and here, with each answer suited to context. | mentions 2:215
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The waw also answers the expectation that banning wine and gambling would remove aid to the poor by directing people to legitimate giving.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-afw is surplus after usual personal and family expenses; the verse directs people to give from that margin instead of committing sins to support the needy. | mentions 7:95
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Spending surplus supports weak Muslims continuously and evenly without hardship, making this a wise social and economic principle.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي ﷺ | reports | A prophetic report calls the best charity that given from sufficiency and says to begin with those one supports.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Supporting dependents prevents them from needing the poor's resources and reduces the number dependent on charity.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p351/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي ﷺ | reports | A prophetic report says leaving heirs wealthy is better than leaving them dependent and begging.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Kadhālika means clarification in this manner, with the demonstrative specifying how God clarifies; Ibn Ashur recalls 2:143. | mentions 2:143
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Alternatively, the demonstrative points to the preceding explanation; its distant form magnifies disclosure of rulings, causes, and a spending principle suited to everyone.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The demonstrative is not directly addressed to the plural, so it stays kadhālika rather than expected kadhālikum; its distance is abstract and honorific.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lām expresses favor and distinction: this lucid teaching lets the community receive duties knowingly and its scholars legislate.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali answers a man disparaging worldly life by describing it as truthful, saving, enriching for those who use it well, and a place of revelation and worship.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352#2/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The matter fit for reflection is the rule on wine and gambling linked to its causes, followed by the related spending instruction.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The definite article marks familiar generic surplus, which varies with each person's ne
