[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This supports voluntary spending: consensus and the wider law require obligatory maintenance and zakat, which may be drawn from surplus wealth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو ذر | reports | Abu Dharr held hoarding wealth forbidden and preached this in Syria; Muawiya complained to Uthman, who recalled him to Medina and settled him at al-Rabadha at his request to avert discord.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قيس بن سعد | reports | Qays ibn Saʿd says the verse concerns obligatory zakat; al- then refers to externally defined growth at the zakat threshold.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read al-afw accusative as object of an understood verb, treating dha after interrogative ma as canceled and ma as yunfiqun's fronted object.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p352/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب | reports | Ibn Kathir in one transmission, Abu Amr, and Yaqub read al-afw nominative as predicate of huwa, taking dha as a relative and matching the answer's case to its construction.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#2/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The impairment of perception and intellect during intoxication and afterward is undeniable, is wine’s greatest sin and corruption, and generates its other corruptions.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#2/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Islamic law protects sound reason and strongly forbids what disables it, including wine, gambling, fraud, and lies; wine and falsehood especially defeat reason’s governance.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Actions and policies built on intoxication and lies threaten humanity and undermine happiness; a law grounded in reason and barring desire that corrupts it is a source of honor.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#2/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Because sensual habits spread quickly and are hard to abandon, God legislates gradually and gently; wine prohibition is one example of that progressive approach.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#3/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Meccan 16:67 mentions intoxicating drink and good provision; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats this as an early, non-explicit stage in wine’s gradual prohibition. | mentions 16:67
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#3/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Medinan 4:43 bars drinking or drunkenness at prayer, limiting it at the best time and place; it precedes al-Baqara and al-Māʾida, since a specific ban after a universal one would reverse the gradual move from ease to severity. | mentions 4:43, 5:90, 5:91
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#3/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Baqara 2:219 came after 4:43 and establishes prohibition by decisively calling wine a great sin, against the background of the earlier Meccan prohibition of sin. | mentions 4:43, 7:33
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#3/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعض المفسرين | rejects | Some exegetes argue that this verse is not explicit in prohibition: sin means harm, and an item with both harm and benefit is not thereby forbidden; they say Companions differed, some abstaining and others continuing while avoiding harm, until al-Māʾida’s explicit ban. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#3/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | First, sin does not simply mean harm; that definition fails for Qur’anic uses of ithm concerning associating partners, a sinful heart, liability for another’s sin, and acquired sins. | mentions 4:48, 2:283, 5:29, 24:11, 4:111
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Kibr compares to size what abundance compares to number; greatness and smallness are relational opposites first understood physically, then extended metaphorically to abstract matters.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The author points to shirk as another sin called great, using the Qur’an’s description in 4:48 when arguing that wine’s sin is especially grave. | mentions 4:48
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | The verse does not explain the ruling merely by harm; even on that assumption, it explicitly says the sin outweighs the benefit, so appeal to independent Companion reasoning contradicts the text.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | Even if 2:219 alone were insufficient to establish prohibition, its explicit naming of sin follows 7:33’s earlier general prohibition; wine is a complete instance of great sin. | mentions 7:33, 4:48
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Qur’an calls killing, concealing testimony, and false accusation sin, but does not call these great sins; it calls wine’s sin great and describes shirk as a great sin. | mentions 4:48
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | After al-Baqara, al-Māʾida 5:90–91 calls wine and gambling satanic pollution and commands avoidance; its closing question shows Muslims had not fully ceased drinking before then. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#4/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Gambling’s social harms and its destruction of the structure of life are visible directly; the author defers fuller discussion to Sūrat al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Benefit and harm describe things sought or avoided for something else, unlike good and evil, which describe things sought or avoided for their own sake.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The benefits people seek in wine and gambling are monetary gains from sale, purchase, and work, along with amusement and pleasure.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Although benefits is plural earlier, the comparison says benefit in the singular: plurality does not affect greatness, so the quantity of benefits is left out of the comparison.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الراغب | reports | Al-Rāghib derives ʿafw from aiming at something to take it, then notes its later senses of forgiveness, effacing traces, and moderation in spending; moderation is intended here.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The intended ʿafw here is the moderate or surplus amount to spend; he adds “God knows best.”
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#5/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The question and answer about what to spend match the earlier question answered by saying that whatever good is spent goes to parents and relatives. | mentions 2:215
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#6/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The invitation to reflection encompasses realities of existence, God and return, nature, society, ethics, and individual and communal life, namely all knowledge tied to human happiness and misery.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#6/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Although the Qur’an commands full obedience to God and His Messenger, it does not approve receiving its rulings and teachings through blind rigidity without thought and reason.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#6/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Tabyīn here means uncovering the reasons behind rulings and clarifying the foundations of teachings and knowledge.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#7/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · علي بن يقطين | reports | Ali ibn Yaqtin recounts the Mahdi questioning Abu al-Hasan about wine's Qur'anic prohibition; the Imam identifies Qur'anic sin with wine and cites 2:219, and the Mahdi acknowledges the Ahl al-Bayt's learning. | mentions 7:33, 2:219
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#7/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أحدهما عليهما السلام | reports | One of the two Imams describes sin as a house with a door and lock, and wine as its key.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls wine the head of every sin.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر عليه السلام | reports | Imam al-Baqir says wine drinkers will be given a hellish drink made from the discharge of prostitutes, which he describes as pus and thick mixed blood.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر عليه السلام | reports | When Quraysh ask which sin is greatest, Imam al-Baqir answers that drinking wine is the greatest.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أحدهما عليهما السلام | reports | One of the two Imams says no act disobeys God more severely than drinking intoxicants, which can lead an unaware drinker to abandon prayer and commit incest.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو عبد الله عليه السلام | reports | Answering why wine is forbidden despite its pleasure, Imam al-Sadiq says it is the mother of abominations and head of evil, removing reason and leading to every sin.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The reports explain one another, and experience and reflection confirm them.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | The Prophet curses ten participants in the wine trade, from its grower and keeper through its drinker, seller, buyer, and consumer of its price.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | The Prophet curses anyone who sits at a table where wine is being drunk.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | The Prophet says God will not look on Judgment Day at four people: a disobedient child, a benefactor who reminds recipients of the gift, a denier of predestination, and a habitual wine drinker.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#8/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | A prophetic report says a wine drinker will receive an equal measure of boiling punishment in the afterlife, whether forgiven or punished, and describes the drinker's appearance on Judgment Day.

9-220#9/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The threats in the wine reports may be supported by the Qur'anic description of the sinner's food and boiling punishment. | mentions 44:43-49
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الباقر عليه السلام | reports | Imam al-Baqir defines al-afw as what remains beyond a year's provision.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r11] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The reported glosses are compatible; the annual-provision account specifies an instance of the meaning.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r12] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Reports on charity's virtues, proper manner, recipients, and amount are too numerous to count and will be cited where relevant later.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو الحسن عليه السلام | reports | Imam al-Rida identifies al-maysir as gambling.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Numerous reports support identifying al-maysir with gambling, a meaning the author regards as beyond doubt.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that companions ordered to spend in God's cause asked how much to give; the verse answered that they should give the surplus, after one man had given away even what he needed to eat.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · يحيى | reports | Yahya reports that Muadh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba, supporting dependents and servants, asked the Prophet how much of their property to spend, prompting the verse.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الصادق عليه السلام | reports | Imam al-Sadiq glosses al-afw as the middle amount.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الباقر والصادق عليهما السلام | reports | Imams al-Baqir and al-Sadiq explain al-afw as enough for subsistence.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو بصير | reports | A report from Abu Basir glosses al-afw as moderation or a reasonable amount.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220#9/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الصادق عليه السلام | reports | Imam al-Sadiq relates the spending verse to the description of those who spend neither extravagantly nor stingily, saying this is the moderate course. | mentions 25:67
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Khamr linguistically means any liquid made to intoxicate; its root sense is covering, since it veils the mind and its ability to distinguish good from evil.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Wine degrades character and leads to obscenity, violence, crimes, murder, divulging secrets, violating rights, and destroying human laws of life, especially protection of honor, life, and property.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The related words khimār, khammartu, and akhmartu refer respectively to a woman’s head covering, covering a vessel, and putting yeast into dough to make it rise.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arabs originally knew wine made from grapes, dates, and barley; later varieties multiplied and all intoxicating kinds, across levels of potency, are khamr.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Maysir means gambling and yāsir means gambler; its root connotes ease because it acquires another’s property without the toil of earning.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A common Arabian form of gambling used arrows or lots to divide a slaughtered camel into twenty-eight shares among ten men; seven winning arrows awarded one to seven shares, while three losing arrows had no share and their holders paid the camel’s cost.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The ten arrows were al-fadhdh, al-tawʾam, al-raqīb, al-ḥils, al-nāfis, al-musbِل, al-muʿallā, al-manīḥ, al-sanīḥ, and al-raghd; the first seven drew assigned shares and the last three drew none.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | reports | A variant reading has kathīr, “much sin,” with thāʾ instead of the written reading kabīr, “great sin.”
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Ithm is close to sin and describes a condition in an act or mind that slows a person from attaining good; wine and gambling have this quality.
[TABATABAI:2:219-220/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Wine causes grave medical harms to the stomach, intestines, liver, lungs, nerves, arteries, heart, and senses, as physicians’ writings and statistics document.
[ASAD-NOTES:2:219#n204/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Ithm literally means sin or anything conducive to sinning; because it is contrasted with benefits, Asad considers “evil” a suitable rendering.
[ASAD-NOTES:2:219#n204/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Razi | reports | Razi and other classical commentators point out that ithm is used as the antithesis of manafiʿ, “benefits.”
[ASAD-NOTES:2:219#n205/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Although this verse says their evil outweighs their benefit, Asad points to the clear prohibition of intoxicants and games of chance in 5:90–91. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The prohibition unfolded in stages: an early Meccan notice of fruit benefits, then a ban on praying while intoxicated, this comparison of harms and benefits, and finally categorical prohibition. | mentions 16:67, 4:43, 5:90
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r10] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Wine’s benefits are commercial and economic returns and temporary pleasure for the user.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r11] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Islam forbids intoxicating drinks and drugs with comparable or greater effects because their harms outweigh limited benefits that can be obtained elsewhere.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r12] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Medina mainly used date-based wine, imported grape wine from Yemen, Taif, and Syria, and also consumed intoxicating raisin/date infusions and drinks made from honey, corn, or barley; intoxicating varieties were called khamr.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r13] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | In Arabic, khamr commonly names all these intoxicating drinks.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r14] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · bazı lugatçılar | reports | Some lexicographers restrict khamr to wine made from unboiled grape juice.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r15] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · bazı fıkıhçılar | reports | Some jurists, following the narrow definition of khamr, held that every amount of grape wine is forbidden but other intoxicants are forbidden only in an intoxicating quantity.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r16] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | After later assessment ended the disagreement, all recognized Islamic legal schools agreed that every amount of any intoxicant is forbidden and may not be consumed.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r17] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Hz. Peygamber | reports | A cited hadith says that a small quantity is forbidden when a large quantity of the substance intoxicates; no grading is stated.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r18] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Hz. Peygamber | reports | A cited hadith says khamr can be made from grape juice, raisins, dates, wheat, barley, or corn, and describes it as what clouds reason and intoxicates; no grading is stated.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r19] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Hz. Peygamber | reports | A cited hadith states that every intoxicant is khamr and every intoxicant is forbidden; no grading is stated.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Hz. Ömer ve birçok sahâbî | reports | Umar and many Companions repeatedly asked for clarification about wine and gambling; their requests are cited among the occasions for the successive explanatory and prohibitory revelations. | mentions 5:90
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r20] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Maysir was named alongside wine because it was entertainment and supplied meat to eat with wine.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r21] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Maysir was played with a camel bought on credit, divided into 28 portions; ten arrows, seven marked with shares and three blank, were drawn, with winners receiving meat shares and losers paying the cost.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r22] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Gambling offered some material benefits through entertainment, food, and drink, but brought far greater sin and harm, including idleness, hostility, neglect of worship, wasted time, lost wealth, and broken households. | mentions 5:91
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r23] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · fıkıhçılar ve tefsirciler | reports | Jurists and exegetes classify all games producing the same result and harms, even if their forms differ, as gambling and forbidden.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r24] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | As wine and gambling began to be prohibited, people who used them to aid the poor asked what to give; God answered “al-afw,” meaning surplus after needs or a suitable part of it.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r25] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | People should meet their own and close relatives’ needs first; providing maintenance to some relatives is a legal and moral duty for those able to do so.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r26] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Ebû Zer el-Gıfârî | reports | Abu Dharr held that surplus wealth may not be hoarded or invested for profit and must go to the needy while they remain.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r27] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · İslâm âlimlerinin büyük çoğunluğu | reports | The majority hold that obligatory transfers are limited to maintenance and zakat; other giving is voluntary, rewarded if done but not sinful to omit.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r28] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The authors conclude that while people lack basic necessities, those who do not help meet those needs remain accountable for their surplus wealth. | mentions 51:19
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r29] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Broadening aid beyond gambling proceeds and zakat to surplus goods, food, and clothing promotes social

 justice and makes unmet basic needs rare.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The extant Torah and Gospels do not appear to prohibit wine.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r4] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Pre-Islamic Arabs prized wine’s intoxication and pleasure and gambling’s entertainment, excitement, hospitality, and aid to the poor, while overlooking the harms.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The verse stresses that wine and gambling do more harm than good; some people therefore gave up wine even before the final prohibition.

[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r8] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | God’s explanations of the wisdom behind commands help people act consciously and apply divine intent without error where no explicit ruling exists.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:219/r9] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Wine can cause addiction, impaired judgment, conflict and mockery, neglect of God and useful activity, waste, and harm to health and future generations.
[QIRAAT-ER:2:219:24#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | The nominative al-ʿafwu reading treats it as subject or predicate, while accusative al-ʿafwa is an object reading, restructuring the syntax.
[QIRAAT-ER:2:219:7#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | The canonical vowel variant changes the hāʾ of fīhimā from kasra to ḍamma, with both dual pronoun forms grammatically valid.
[QIRAAT-ER:2:219:9#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | A dot variant changes bāʾ to thāʾ, changing k-b-r greatness to k-th-r abundance: the sin is abundant rather than great.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The prohibition of drinking wine is discussed at 4:43. | mentions 4:43
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r10] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Later legal philosophy treated protecting intelligence as one of the Law’s essential objectives, partly through its ruling on intoxication.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r11] STUDYQURAN · R | reports | Gambling creates enmity and despair, yields ill-gotten gains, and diverts people from wholesome pursuit of profit.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r12] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Islamic financial theory invalidates some transactions for excessive risk; theorists relate that risk to the prohibition of ribā, which some discuss as a severe form of risk. | mentions 2:275, 2:276, 2:277, 2:278, 2:279, 2:280
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r13] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Al-ʿafw means what is easy or done without difficulty, and in other contexts can mean pardon or forgiveness.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r14] STUDYQURAN · author | reports | Commentators disagree whether the spending command concerns voluntary charity or a required duty.

[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r16] STUDYQURAN · Others | reports | Others see no contradiction between zakāh and a continuing command to give charity.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r17] STUDYQURAN · Commentators | reports | Charitable giving should avoid both miserliness and wastefulness and should not impoverish the giver.
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r18] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | This verse expands on 2:215 by addressing how much to give, complementing that verse’s account of charity’s recipients. | mentions 2:215
[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r19] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The proper extent of charitable giving is also addressed in 17:29. | mentions 17:29

[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r3] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | In maysir, players draw arrows to divide meat; the loser pays without receiving meat and is mocked, while winners give their shares to the poor as generosity.

[STUDYQURAN:2:219/r5] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Chess and backgammon came to the West from the Islamic world and remain popular among Muslims, including many devout people.

[MUJAHID:v1p106/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | Mujahid calls this the first occasion on which wine was censured.
[MUJAHID:v1p106/r2] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | The benefits are what people gain from wine and gambling.
[MUJAHID:v1p106/r3] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | Maysir means gambling; its name is linked to the expression aysiru, meaning to slaughter or divide an animal, as in a wager to put up set amounts.
[MUJAHID:v1p106/r4] MUJAHID, d. 104 · طاوس | reports | Tawus interprets al-afw, the amount to spend, as maysir.
[MUJAHID:v1p106/r5] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | Mujahid interprets al-afw as the obligatory alms.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The verse was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and several Helpers; maysir means gambling.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | In the gambling game, a group bought a camel by shares and drew lots; the person whose lot came out paid the whole price but received no meat, which the others divided.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Their sin lies in neglecting prayer and remembrance of God and committing forbidden acts through drinking and gambling.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Before prohibition, their benefits were pleasure and trade; gambling could benefit some while causing others, the gamblers, to lose.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The sin after prohibition outweighs the benefits before it; their prohibition was revealed a year after this verse.
[MUQATIL:2:219-220/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Maysir was named from their phrase yassirū lanā thamana al-jazūr, meaning make the camel's price easy for us.
[FARRA:v1p140/r8] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | العفو is the surplus wealth one spends; al-Farrāʾ says the zakāt obligation later abrogated this ruling.
[MAJAZ:v1p73/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-maysir means gambling.
[MAJAZ:v1p73/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is what one can afford, and also moderation or what is readily clear for one; take what is easy and available to you.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · مجاهد وقتادة | reports | Mujahid and Qatada report that when this verse came, some people continued drinking and others abstained, until wine was prohibited in al-Maʾida.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada defines al-maysir as gambling.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · مجاهد وسعيد | reports | Mujahid and Saʿid define all gambling as maysir, including children’s game of walnuts.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r4] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿud warns against playing with dice or knucklebones, calling them a form of gambling.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r5] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses al-ʿafw as surplus wealth.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p88/r6] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says reflection on this world and the next lets people recognize the superiority of the afterlife over worldly life.
[AKHFASH:v1p185/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | If ماذا is treated as ما alone, العفو is accusative as the object of ينفقون: the question is what they spend, and the answer is that they spend surplus.
[AKHFASH:v1p185/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | If ذا is the relative الذي, العفو is nominative as the predicate: what they spend is surplus; compare the two analyses of ماذا in 16:24 and 16:30. | mentions 16:24, 16:30
[AKHFASH:v1p185/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The alternative case can also be licensed by meaning: a nominative answer can mean 'what I did was good,' while an accusative answer can mean 'I did good.'
[AKHFASH:v1p185/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | In the poem دعي ماذا علمت, ما and ذا together mean ما alone; taking ذا as الذي would make دعي ما الذي علمت ungrammatical.
[AKHFASH:v1p185/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · أهل التأويل | reports | Exegetes say the disbelievers denied that God sent anything and asked what the people themselves claimed was revealed; the author finds this like 'they are your brothers' in 2:220. | mentions 16:24, 2:220
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p82#3/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Al-maysir means gambling; Ibn Qutayba refers readers to his discussion of its benefit in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p82#3/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The question asks what they should give in charity.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p82#3/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is the surplus beyond one's own and dependents' sustenance; it can also mean what comes easily, without compulsion or hardship.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p82#3/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The command to accept what people freely volunteer means not to press them for more than they offer. | mentions 7:199
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā ibn Thaʿlaba’s camel-wager poem, beginning “wa-jazūru aysārin,” illustrates the camel meat won in maysir.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid identifies the benefits of maysir as the portions of the camel won in gambling.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says wine’s benefits were pleasure and price, while maysir’s were its gambling winnings.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the benefits of wine and gambling mentioned here were those they had before the two were prohibited.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas says the benefit was the pleasure and joy people experienced when drinking wine.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عظم أهل المدينة وبعض الكوفيين والبصريين | prefers | Most Medinese readers and some Kufans and Basrans read kabīr with bāʾ, meaning a grave or great sin.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون من أهل البصرة والكوفة | rejects | Other Basran and Kufan readers understood the reading as denoting many sins, taking the singular ithm in a collective sense.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Tabari prefers the great-sin reading: agreement on akbar, “greater,” shows magnitude, whereas a numerical comparison would say akthar, “more.”
[TAB-FULL:v3p676#2/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | The comparative phrase “their sin is greater than their benefit” confirms that the earlier description means greatness, not a greater number of sins.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says wine’s sin is that intoxication makes a person harm others, while gambling’s sin is withholding rights and injustice.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid calls this the first criticism directed at wine.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas explains wine’s sin as the loss of religion suffered by its drinker.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Tabari prefers that wine’s grave sin is loss of reason through intoxication, until the drinker loses awareness of his Lord; he takes this to be Ibn ʿAbbas’s meaning.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The sin in gambling is distraction from remembering God and prayer, and the enmity and hatred that arise between gamblers. | mentions 5:91
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Before prohibition, wine’s benefits included its price and the pleasure of drinking it.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā’s poem contrasts wine’s morning gloom and sorrow with evening pleasure and abundant wealth, as evidence of its worldly benefits.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Ḥassān’s verse says wine leaves its drinkers kings and lions, illustrating the pleasure and perceived benefit people found in it.
[TAB-FULL:v3p676/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Gambling’s benefit was the share of camel meat won by the players, who wagered on a camel, slaughtered it when a player won, and divided it into ten lots according to the arrows.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The harms of drinking wine and gambling exceed their gains: drunkenness led people to attack and fight, while gambling brought strife that led them into sin.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verse was revealed before explicit prohibition, and the sin attributed to wine and maysir is the sin caused by them, not a later sin of violating the ban.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | rejects | Ibn ʿAbbas is reported to say that the benefits were before prohibition and the sin came after prohibition; Tabari rejects this chronology.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع | rejects | Al-Rabīʿ likewise places the benefits before prohibition and the sin after it, an interpretation Tabari rejects.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك | rejects | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the sin after prohibition exceeds the benefit before it; Tabari rejects this reading of the verse.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | A further report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the loss to religion from wine exceeds the pleasure gained from drinking it.
[TAB-FULL:v3p679/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr recounts the staged response: some avoided wine after 2:219 while others drank for its benefits; 4:43 restricted drinking around prayer, and 5:90 then ordered its avoidance, prompting ʿUmar’s exclamation. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p682/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar recounts three stages: 2:219 first, then 4:43 forbidding prayer while drunk, and finally 5:90, after which the Messenger declared wine forbidden. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p682/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة والحسن | reports | ʿIkrima and al-Ḥasan say the wine pas

[TAB-FULL:v3p682/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو القموص زيد بن علي | reports | Abū al-Qamūṣ says wine was revealed about in three stages: after 2:219, some Muslims drank; two intoxicated men spoke incoherently in prayer, prompting 4:43, and another drinker later began lamenting the Badr dead. | mentions 4:43
[TAB-FULL:v3p683/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو القموص زيد بن علي | reports | Abū al-Qamūṣ’s report continues with the man’s verse lament for Badr’s dead; the Messenger rushed to him, he vowed never to drink again, and 5:90–91 prohibited wine, whereupon ʿUmar said they had stopped. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[TAB-FULL:v3p683/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī counts four wine passages: 2:219, the passage at 16:67 after which people drank, and the final prohibition in 5:90–91. | mentions 16:67, 5:90, 5:91
[TAB-FULL:v3p683/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says drinking continued after 2:219; an intoxicated recitation at ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf’s meal led to 4:43, and later a drunken dispute at Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ’s meal led to 5:90–91 and prohibition. | mentions 4:43, 5:90, 5:91
[TAB-FULL:v3p685/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة ومجاهد | reports | Qatada and a transmitter from Mujahid say that after this verse some people drank wine and others abstained until its prohibition in Sūrat al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p685/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid again describes this as the first criticism directed at wine.
[TAB-FULL:v3p685/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the verse initially disparaged wine and gambling without banning them; 4:43 then prohibited drunkenness around prayer, and after al-Aḥzāb 5:90 prohibited wine in every amount, whether intoxicating or not. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p685/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع | reports | Al-Rabīʿ transmits that the Prophet called each successive revelation a sign that God was advancing the prohibition of wine, until it became forbidden. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p686/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says the passage was superseded by three verses in al-Māʾida and discusses the Prophet’s wine punishment: he treated it as a hadd by his judgment, not a fixed, named hadd. | mentions 5:90
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The companions ask what portion of their wealth to give as charity; God answers that they should give al-ʿafw.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r10] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan also defines al-ʿafw as a middle level of spending: do not exhaust your wealth in giving it away.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas glosses al-ʿafw as what remains after one’s household support.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says al-ʿafw means surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ also glosses al-ʿafw as surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī likewise glosses al-ʿafw as surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan glosses al-ʿafw as surplus wealth.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says people should give what remains from that day’s earnings after providing for their families, without leaving them hungry.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | A second gloss from Ibn ʿAbbas is whatever does not show noticeably in one’s property.
[TAB-FULL:v3p687/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · طاوس | reports | Ṭāwūs says al-ʿafw is a small amount from each thing.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Muhammad’s companions ask what wealth to give in charity, and God directs them to give al-ʿafw.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r10] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers the surplus remaining after a person’s own, family, and necessary expenses; this is what the Prophet permitted as charity.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ says al-ʿafw is an amount that does not exhaust one’s wealth and force one to ask others.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ also explains al-ʿafw as spending without extravagance or miserliness in what is right.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid defines al-ʿafw as charity given while one remains comfortably provided for.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says al-ʿafw means not exhausting one’s wealth.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says to accept whatever people bring, whether little or much.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع | reports | Al-Rabīʿ interprets al-ʿafw as the good, best, and purest part of one’s wealth.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says al-ʿafw is the surplus, the best of one’s wealth.
[TAB-FULL:v3p689/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid is also reported as identifying al-ʿafw with obligatory charity; Abū ʿĀṣim is uncertain in the transmission from Qays.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو هريرة | reports | A man with one dinar is told to spend it on himself, then to provide for his family and child; with another remaining, he may decide what to do.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · جابر بن عبد الله | reports | The Prophet instructs a poor person to begin with himself, then dependents, and then charity to others if anything remains.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · جابر بن عبد الله | reports | A man offers the Prophet a gold egg that is all he owns; the Prophet rejects this all-in charity and says charity is from sufficiency.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله | reports | The Prophet says to give from surplus, begin with those one supports, and that a person is not blamed for keeping sufficient means.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | These reports show that the Prophet permitted charity from surplus after need; al-Ṭabarī identifies that surplus as al-ʿafw.
[TAB-FULL:v3p692/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, al-ʿafw in wealth and other things means increase and abundance; al-Ṭabarī cites the phrase in 7:95 as an example. | mentions 7:95
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The poem’s description of fat-rich animals illustrates ʿāfiyāt as abundant in fat, supporting the sense of plenty.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The idiom “take what is left freely for you” means take what remains in excess after the other person’s effort; this supports al-ʿafw as surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Prophet’s statement that the best charity is given from sufficiency confirms al-Ṭabarī’s surplus interpretation.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Ṭabarī rejects equating al-ʿafw with obligatory zakāt: after neglect, even a person whose remaining property is only the zakāt due must pay it, which is exertion rather than surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | He also rejects the view that al-ʿafw means whatever amount the owner gives, because that could include the whole wealth and so be exertion, not surplus.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي | reports | When Abū Lubābah offers to give away his wealth in repentance, the Prophet says a third is enough; a similar report is transmitted about Kaʿb ibn Mālik. Al-Ṭabarī uses this against defining al-ʿafw as wealth whose surplus is not apparent.
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw is measured moderation: the amount the Prophet set according to one’s wealth and capacity, between extravagance and miserliness, as urged in 25:67 and 17:29. | mentions 25:67, 17:29
[TAB-FULL:v3p693/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل العلم | reports | Some scholars say the verse was abrogated by the obligatory zakāt; the dispute continues in the following segments.
[TAB-FULL:v3p694/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says this instruction came before charity was made obligatory.
[TAB-FULL:v3p694/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says no fixed amount was prescribed at first; 7:199 followed, and named obligations were revealed afterward. | mentions 7:199
[TAB-FULL:v3p694/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says zakāt abrogated this instruction.
[TAB-FULL:v3p694/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | Other scholars hold that the verse remains in force and was not abrogated.
[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī holds, following Ibn ʿAbbās as transmitted by ʿAṭiyya, that this is guidance about approved voluntary giving, not a divine obligation; it remains in force and is neither superseded nor superseding.
[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | This etiquette governs voluntary alms, gifts, and grants: spend first on oneself, family, and children, then direct remaining surplus to pleasing purposes.
[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The proper amount is balance between extravagance and stinginess, as described in the Qur’an’s account of moderate spending. | mentions 25:67
[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Ṭabarī argues abrogation is unproven: scholars agree a person may give charity, gifts, and bequests up to a third, and no evidence shows this guidance was once obligatory and then removed by zakāt.
[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قراء الحجاز، قراء الحرمين، عظم قراء الكوفيين، بعض قراء البصريين | reports | Most Hijazi, Ḥaramayn, and Kufan readers pronounce al-ʿafw accusative; some Basrans read it nominative. Both readings are sound, but al-Ṭabarī prefers accusative because it is more widely read and renowned.

[TAB-FULL:v3p695/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says the alternative parses are also valid Arabic: accusative al-ʿafw with mādhā as two words, or nominative al-ʿafw with mādhā as one.
[TAB-FULL:v4p693#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | As God clarified the direction and limits of spending in His way, He clarifies other signs, their rulings, lawful and forbidden matters, and their proofs as a favor to people.
[TAB-FULL:v4p693#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The invitation to reflect means using reason to consider God's proofs, take heed, act on their rulings, and thereby obey Him.
[TAB-FULL:v4p693#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid glosses the phrase as “that you obey.” | mentions 2:266
[TAB-FULL:v4p693#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says reflection concerns the world's passing and perishing and the hereafter's coming and permanence.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine is the agreed case; by analogy, anything that acts like it is also called khamr and has the same prohibition.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Khamr is named from covering: it applies to what veils a person, a woman’s veil, a prayer mat covering the face, and dough covered by fermentation.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | All intoxicants are khamr because they mix with and cover the intellect, whatever name they are given; drinkers are described as intoxicated or suffering a hangover.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أبو الأسود الدؤلي | reports | After someone claimed a differently named intoxicant was lawful, Abū al-Aswad recognized it as wine’s kin; his poem says the two are siblings nurtured by the same mother.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قراء | reports | A variant reading has kathīr (‘much’) in place of kabīr (‘great’) in the phrase about sin.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قوم | reports | Some say this verse only discouraged wine and gambling, with their prohibition made explicit later in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:90, 5:91
[ZAJJAJ:v1p291/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قوم | reports | Others say the prohibition is already conveyed here and is clarified by the Book elsewhere.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine is prohibited by the Qur’anic text because it is called a great sin, and God explicitly forbids sin; Zajjāj cites 7:33 despite consensus. | mentions 7:33
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r10] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw may also be nominative with compound mā-dhā, understood as the predicate in, Say: it is the surplus.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r11] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw means surplus or abundance; ʿafā al-qawm describes a people who became numerous.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r12] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | People were commanded to give away surplus until alms tax was prescribed; consensus holds zakat rules specify dues on the kinds of property.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r13] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Exegetical reports describe earners keeping enough income and owners of gold and silver keeping a year's provision, then donating the remainder.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine causes enmity and hatred and obstructs reason, by which one distinguishes things and recognizes duties toward the Creator.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Gambling breeds enmity and hatred, and transfers a person's property to another without compensation.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wine's benefits include pleasure and profit from trading in it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Gambling can bring a person property without toil or effort.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The sin in wine and gambling outweighs their benefits.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Both accusative and nominative are possible for al-ʿafw when mā-dhā is treated as one noun and al-ʿafw is referred back to it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | If mā is a noun and dhā a predicate meaning alladhī, al-ʿafw is nominative as the answer to what they spend.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p292/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-ʿafw may be accusative as the object of yunfiqun: spend the surplus, even when mā is a noun by itself.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The clarification about wine and gambling exemplifies how God makes His signs clear.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The Prophet's address also addresses his community; singular address followed by a plural is common in Arabic and frequent in the Qur’an. | mentions 65:1
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | A plural group can be treated as a collective tribe and referred to with singular dhālika; the Qur’an likewise uses dhālika after addressing the Prophet's wives with minkunna. | mentions 33:30
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | In this world and the next may attach to you reflect, meaning reflect on the affairs of both worlds.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p293/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Alternatively, in this world and the next may attach to God clarifies the signs, meaning signs concerning both worlds are clarified so people reflect.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر | reports | Umar repeatedly prayed for clarification about wine; revelation progressed from 2:219 to the prayer restriction in 4:43 and the final prohibition in 5:90-91, after which he declared that they abstained because wine wastes wealth and reason. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the statement about sin and benefits in this verse was abrogated by the final prohibition in 5:90. | mentions 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar recounts three stages: this verse, then the ban on approaching prayer intoxicated, then the final prohibition, which the Prophet announced as making wine forbidden. | mentions 4:43, 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar says wine's prohibition concerned products of grapes, honey, dates, wheat, and barley, and defines wine as whatever overwhelms the intellect.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p388#2/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports that people drank wine after the initial verse, then left it when the prohibition in al-Ma'ida was announced; their drink was date nabidh called fadikh. | mentions 5:90
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab explains the name wine by saying its clear part rises while its dregs sink.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar defines maysir as gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid defines maysir as gambling and connects its name to the expression about staking or dividing a camel.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عبد الله بن مسعود، ابن عباس، عطاء، طاووس، سعيد بن جبير، الحسن، ابن سيرين، قتادة، مقاتل، السدي، عطاء الخراساني | reports | Abu Muhammad reports these authorities as agreeing with Mujahid that maysir means gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · النبي، أبو موسى الأشعري | reports | The Prophet says to avoid marked dice used for casting lots, since they are maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عبد الله بن مسعود، علي، ابن عمر، عائشة | reports | Ibn Masud calls dice non-Arab maysir and warns against them; Ali, Ibn Umar, and Aisha are reported similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali says chess is a form of maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab says a form of pre-Islamic maysir was selling meat for one or two sheep.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p390/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · القاسم بن محمد | reports | Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad says backgammon is maysir whenever it distracts from remembrance of God and prayer.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الأعرج | reports | Al-Araj defines maysir as casting arrows for stakes of property and fruit.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · النبي | reports | A report from the Prophet lists betting over pigeons, gambling, and throwing dice as three forms of maysir.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says their great sin is the religious loss incurred by buying them.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains their sin as neglecting prayer and remembrance of God through wine and gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the benefits of wine are the pleasure and joy people get from drinking it.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains the benefits as the price of wine and the camel meat people obtained through gambling.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن أبي زائدة | reports | A transmission from Mujahid through Ibn Abi Zayda differs, identifying the benefit as wine's price before prohibition.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · شبل، ابن جريج | reports | Shibl and Ibn Jurayj support the report that the benefits included what people obtained from the camel.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p391/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the verse censured wine and gambling for their greater sin without yet forbidding them; Muslims then drank wine lawfully for its benefits.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas di

[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says their sin outweighs their benefits because of the loss to religion, despite the pleasure and enjoyment people gain.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مقاتل بن حيان | reports | Muqatil contrasts the greater sin after prohibition with the benefits they had before prohibition.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · معاذ بن جبل، ثعلبة | reports | A report says Muadh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba, concerned about their dependents, asked the Prophet what they should spend, occasioning the spending question in this verse.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس، عبد الله بن عمر، مجاهد، عطاء، الحسن، عكرمة، محمد بن كعب، قتادة، القاسم، سالم، سعيد بن جبير، عطاء الخراساني، الربيع بن أنس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains al-afw as what remains after providing for one's family; many listed authorities are reported similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · طاوس عن مجاهد | reports | A report through Mujahid from Tawus defines al-afw as the easy or readily available portion of everything.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p392/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | Al-Rabi explains al-afw as the good portion of one's wealth, its best and finest part.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد عن قيس المكي | reports | A report through Qays al-Makki says Mujahid defined al-afw as the obligatory charity.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says al-afw is surplus wealth and that this instruction came before charity was prescribed.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p393/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي، عطاء الخراساني، أبو محمد | reports | Al-Suddi interprets al-afw as surplus wealth and says the command was abrogated by zakat; Ata al-Khurasani is reported similarly.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan takes the instruction to mean: spend the surplus.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The reflection invited here concerns both worldly life and the Hereafter.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | Al-Ḥaramayn and Abū ʿAmr read kabīr, while the Kufans read kathīr; kabīr is preferable, matching ṣaghīr/kabīr and the established pair kabāʾir/ṣaghāʾir. | mentions 4:2
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | The Ḥaramayn and Kufans read al-ʿafw accusative, while Abū ʿAmr, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read nominative; both are grammatical, but the verse’s interpretation favors accusative.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | If dhā means “that which,” nominative is preferred but accusative is allowed; if mādhā is one word, accusative is preferred but nominative is allowed. Both occur in the question ماذا تعلمت أنحوا أم شعرا.
[NAHHAS:v1p308/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains al-ʿafw as the surplus.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The reading with bāʾ, kabīr, is supported by the next phrase's akbar rather than akthar.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The reading with thāʾ, kathīr, suits the counted items of consumed wine and gambling; a verse elsewhere uses akthar for degree or amount. | mentions 6:59
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | With rafʿ, mā and dhā are separate: dhā is relative, and al-ʿafw is the predicate answering what they should spend.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | With naṣb, mādhā is one interrogative word and al-ʿafw is the object of yanfiqūn.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p96/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Mā and dhā combine because both are general and ambiguous, covering rational and non-rational things; man is restricted to rational beings, so man and dhā do not combine.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr with thāʾ; the rest read kabīr with bāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سعيد عن قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the verse condemned wine without prohibiting it while it was lawful; the prayer and later al-Māʾida verses then prohibited every amount. | mentions 4:43
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أهل النظر | reports | Some scholars infer prohibition because God forbids sin in 7:33 and this verse calls wine and gambling a great sin. | mentions 7:33
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī also reads the sin as arising in deeming wine and gambling lawful; only some qualities of otherwise ordinary things are forbidden.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa says looking at wine for sensual enjoyment is itself forbidden.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The sin refers to sinful acts committed through wine and gambling and the causes leading to them.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p307/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · بعض نقلة الآثار | reports | Transmitters report that this verse descended without prohibiting wine; reports differ on whether prohibition came here or in al-Māʾida.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p309/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī says ithm can denote appropriated property; ‘sin or offense’ distinguishes a wrong against God from a wrong against people, and the verse arose over theft. | mentions 4:112, 5:107
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p310/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Taʾaththama and taḥawwaba mean avoiding sin although their forms might suggest committing it, like tafawwaqa and tajarraʿa.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Labīd’s h-j-d forms contrast sleeping with staying awake; the Qurʾān uses tahajjud for night prayer, illustrating the specialized sense. | mentions 17:79
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | prefers | Al-Fārisī favors kabīr: great sin contrasts with small sin, matching kabāʾir and akbar; great sin is also ʿaẓīm, while kathīr would contrast with qalīl. | mentions 54:53, 53:32, 4:31, 31:13, 4:48
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p312/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The thāʾ reading is supported by the warning that wine and gambling produce enmity and obstruct remembrance and prayer. | mentions 5:91
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The Prophetic report about ten persons involved with wine being cursed supports the kathīr reading.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أنس بن مالك عن النبي | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet cursed ten people involved in wine, including buyers, sellers, producers, carriers, servers, and those who consume its price.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Even if harms arise from effects of wine and gambling, revelation assigns blame to them; gambling includes wrongful taking of wealth. | mentions 5:91, 4:29
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Since sin is balanced against benefits, kathīr naturally means many harms, like the Qurʾānic description of numerous livestock benefits. | mentions 23:21
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p314/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Wine is not linguistically identical to nabīdh; primary names are not assigned by analogy, as Abū al-Aswad’s poem calls wine its sister.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Abū ʿAmr alone reads al-ʿafw nominative; others read it accusative, also reported from Ibn ʿĀmir. A Meccan transmission from Ibn Kathīr has nominative, though Meccans now read accusative.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās defines al-ʿafw as what remains beyond the family’s needs.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عطاء وقتادة والسدي | reports | ʿAṭāʾ, Qatāda, and al-Suddī define al-ʿafw as surplus.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says it is the non-straining good surplus of one’s wealth, excluding the principal.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda defines it as affordable capacity or moderation and connects it to what is clear or available.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · غيره | reports | Another authority glosses al-ʿafw as wealth beyond one’s exertion.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Mādhā can be one compound interrogative noun; retaining the alif in ʿammā dhā tasʾalu shows mā is not word-final, unlike ʿamma and fīma. | mentions 78:1, 79:43
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Alternatively, dhā can mean ‘that which’; a cited poem uses mādhā in that sense.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p315/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In the poet’s question about the women, mādhā functions like mā alone; parsing dhā as a relative pronoun is unnatural.
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Wine and gambling are described as matters of conjecture and deception.
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · طاوس وسالم | reports | On 36:55, they remarked that knowing whom the people of Paradise were distracted from would have changed how they enjoyed their occupation. | mentions 36:55
[SULAMI:v1p73#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Some people become transformed by the Divine Presence without realizing it.
[THALABI:v2p141/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب ومعاذ بن جبل | reports | Umar, Muadh, and several Ansar asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine and gambling, saying they destroy reason and consume wealth; the verse was revealed in response.
[THALABI:v2p141/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The source describes staged prohibition: an earlier Meccan verse mentioned intoxicating drink from dates and grapes, when Muslims still drank lawfully; 2:219 then identified the greater sin. | mentions 1

[THALABI:v2p141/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said God was moving toward prohibiting wine; some abandoned it, while others continued for its benefits and tried to avoid its harms.
[THALABI:v2p141/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | At Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's meal, companions became intoxicated; the prayer leader recited Surat al-Kafirun but omitted la, prompting the ban on prayer while drunk. | mentions 4:43
[THALABI:v2p141/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | After the prayer incident, Umar said successive warnings suggested wine would soon be prohibited altogether; some abandoned it because it interfered with prayer. | mentions 4:43
[THALABI:v2p142/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Some continued drinking outside prayer. One Muslim drank, lamented those killed at Badr in verse, and vowed never to drink again when the Prophet rushed over angrily.
[THALABI:v2p142/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · علي | reports | Ali reports that intoxicated Hamza slaughtered and ate Ali's camels, which Ali planned to sell to fund his marriage to Fatima; Hamza insulted Ali's lineage, and the Prophet compensated him.
[THALABI:v2p143/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The morning after Hamza's drunken attack, he apologized; the Prophet said he had asked God, who had forgiven him.
[THALABI:v2p143/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · سعد بن أبي وقاص | reports | Atban's feast included wine and drunken boasting; Saʿd recited a poem insulting the Ansar, and an Ansari wounded him with a camel jawbone.
[THALABI:v2p143/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | After Saʿd complained, Umar prayed for a clear ruling; final prohibition came in al-Maida days after the Trench, and Umar declared they had stopped. | mentions 5:90
[THALABI:v2p143/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس | reports | Anas says wine was cherished but, at its prohibition, people poured it into streets or broke and washed vessels; after rain Medina's alleys smelled of wine. | mentions 5:90
[THALABI:v2p143/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان الثوري وأبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف وأكثر أهل الرأي | reports | This legal school narrowly defines khamr as naturally fermented grape or date juice, without fire; other drinks are not khamr by name.
[THALABI:v2p143/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان الثوري وأبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف وأكثر أهل الرأي | reports | They say cooked juice is lawful though disliked after two-thirds evaporate; when two-thirds evaporate and one-third remains, drinking and selling are allowed unless intoxicating.
[THALABI:v2p143/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | They support this with Abu Hurayra's report that the Prophet said wine comes from the date palm and grapevine.
[THALABI:v2p144/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Ibn Sirin reports Umar told an official to cook the drink until two-thirds evaporated, leaving one share for people and removing the devil's two shares.
[THALABI:v2p144/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Burda ibn Sahl reports the Prophet told people to drink from vessels but not to become intoxicated.
[THALABI:v2p144/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عبد الرحمن السدي | rejects | Al-Suddi calls that hadith munkar: Abu al-Ahwas erred, Samak's companions did not rely on him, and Samak was weak and accepted prompting.
[THALABI:v2p144/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · أحمد | rejects | Ahmad says Abu al-Ahwas erred; Sharik differs in chain and wording, reporting that the Prophet prohibited several vessel types.
[THALABI:v2p144/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · قرصافة عن عائشة | reports | They also invoke a report attributed to Aisha through Qursafa that permits drinking if one does not become intoxicated.
[THALABI:v2p144/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports a story that Noah and Satan disputed ownership of the grapevine and settled that Noah would have one-third and Satan two-thirds.
[THALABI:v2p144/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib identifies the drink Umar permitted as one cooked until two-thirds evaporated and one-third remained.
[THALABI:v2p144/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · موسى الأموي | reports | Musa al-Umawi is reported to have drunk tala after two-thirds evaporated and one-third remained.
[THALABI:v2p144/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says tala cooked down to one-third is unobjectionable; al-Miswar agrees.
[THALABI:v2p144/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | Al-Thaʿlabi understands these reports to concern a nonintoxicating remainder; he cites Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's order and rule that every intoxicant is forbidden.
[THALABI:v2p144/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told officials not to drink tala until two-thirds evaporated and added that every intoxicant is forbidden.
[THALABI:v2p144/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · إسماعيل بن علية وجماعة من أهل العراق | reports | Some say even slight cooking makes juice tala; Ismail ibn Ulayya and a group of Iraqis hold this view.
